source: Dionysii Cartusiani Opera Omnia, t. VII (Montreuil)

1.title: AN LIBER ISTE AD LITTERAM EXPONENDUS SIT DE DEO ET SYNAGOGA, VEL POTIUS DE CHRISTO ET ECCLESIA.
1.title_en: Whether this book is to be expounded literally of God and the Synagogue, or rather of Christ and the Church

paras.t: In omni scientia oportet in primis scire, quæ sit materia seu subjectum aut genus scibile libri illius scientiæ : sic jam de libro isto necesse est cognoscere, de quo tractet. Et de hoc sic narrat Nicolaus de Lyra : Hebræi dicunt, quod liber iste loquitur parabolice de amore Dei et plebis Judaicæ, quam sibi desponsavit in legis datione, sicque habuit eam in sponsam prædilectam. Expositores vero catholici dicunt communiter, quod liber iste loquitur parabolice de amore Christi et Ecclesiæ, accipiendo Ecclesiam prout dividitur contra Synagogam : quæ Ecclesia processit de latere Christi dormientis in cruce, sicut Eva formata fuit de costa dormientis Adæ. Et sic tam isti, quam illi, nituntur ad suas intentiones litteram applicare. Sed salvo meliori judicio, utrique videntur in aliquo deficere. Primo, quod sponsam accipiunt nimis stricte Judæi, dicentes sponsam esse præcise plebem Hebraicam cum plebe conversa ad ipsam, Catholici vero plebem christianam : quia in hoc libro ponuntur aliqua, quæ non videntur convenienter exponi, referendo ad statum veteris Testamenti ; et econverso aliqua, quæ non possunt exponi convenienter de statu novi. Ex hoc sequitur defectus alius, quo Judæi aliqua ad statum novi pertinentia, inconvenienter exponunt de statu veteris ; et econverso Catholici aliqua ad vetus Testamentum pertinentia, minus convenienter exponunt de statu novi. Hæc Lyra.
paras.en: In every science one must first of all know what is the matter, or subject, or knowable class [genus scibile, that is, the kind of thing which that science knows about] of the book of that science: so now, of this book, it is necessary to know what it treats of. And on this Nicholas of Lyra relates as follows: The Hebrews say that this book speaks in parables of the love of God and of the Jewish people, whom He espoused to Himself in the giving of the Law, and so had her as His beloved bride. But the Catholic expositors commonly say that this book speaks in parables of the love of Christ and the Church, taking the Church as it is set apart from the Synagogue: which Church came forth from the side of Christ sleeping on the cross[[John 19:34||]], as Eve was formed from the rib of the sleeping Adam[[Gen 2:21||]][[Gen 2:22||]]. And so both the one party and the other strive to fit the letter to their own purposes. But, saving a better judgment, both seem to fall short in some respect. First, in that they take the bride too narrowly: the Jews saying that the bride is precisely the Hebrew people, together with the people converted to it, and the Catholics that she is the Christian people; for in this book some things are set down which it seems cannot fittingly be explained by referring them to the state of the Old Testament, and conversely some which cannot fittingly be explained of the state of the New. From this follows another defect: the Jews unfittingly explain of the state of the Old some things that belong to the state of the New; and conversely the Catholics, less fittingly, explain of the state of the New some things that belong to the Old Testament. Thus far Lyra.

paras.t: Cujus verba non videntur idonea, quibus ait indeterminate, quod catholici expositores dicunt hunc librum loqui de amore Christi et Ecclesiæ, accipiendo Ecclesiam prout contra Synagogam dividitur. Antiqui enim et sancti præcipuique expositores, affirmant hunc librum tractare de Christo atque Ecclesia, prout Ecclesia Synagogam includit, imo prout designat electorum omnium ab exordio mundi congregationem et cœtum electorum. Etenim Origenes, qui tam eleganter super Cantica scripsit, ut Hieronymus protestetur, quod quamvis in ceteris scriptis cunctos, qui ante eum fuerunt, doctores excesserit, tamen super hæc Cantica se ipso excellentior fuit, ait : Ecclesia sit desiderans Christo conjungi (Ecclesiam autem, cœtum omnium adverte sanctorum) : hæc ergo Ecclesia sit quasi una omnium persona, quæ loquatur et dicat : Omnia habeo; repleta sum muneribus, quæ sponsaliorum titulo ante nuptias sumpsi. Dudum enim dum præpararer ad conjugium filii Regis, primogeniti omnis creaturæ, ministraverunt mihi angeli sancti ejus, deferentes ad me legem sponsalis muneris loco. Hæc Origenes. Certum est autem, istud non convenire Ecclesiæ, nisi ex persona et parte Synagogæ.
paras.en: His words, in which he says without qualification that the Catholic expositors say this book speaks of the love of Christ and the Church, taking the Church as it is set apart from the Synagogue, do not seem apt. For the ancient, holy and principal expositors affirm that this book treats of Christ and the Church as the Church includes the Synagogue, nay rather as it signifies the gathering of all the elect from the beginning of the world, the company of the elect. For Origen, who wrote so finely on the Canticles that Jerome declares that, though in his other writings he surpassed all the doctors who were before him, yet on these Canticles he surpassed himself, says: Let the Church be one who longs to be joined to Christ (and by the Church understand the company of all the saints): let this Church, then, be as it were one person made of all, who speaks and says: I have all things; I am filled with gifts, which I received before the marriage by title of betrothal. For long ago, while I was being prepared for wedlock with the Son of the King, the Firstborn of every creature, His holy angels ministered to me, bringing me the Law in place of a betrothal gift. Thus far Origen. Now it is certain that this does not befit the Church except in the person and on the part of the Synagogue.

paras.t: Insuper Anselmus Cantuariensis archiepiscopus in prologo suo super Cantica, scripsit : Sub prophetia (quæ fit de præterito, ac præsenti, et futuro) liber iste supponi dicitur, quia ostendit cum quanto desiderio fidelis Synagoga adventum Christi desiderabat et exspectabat : quod modo transactum est. Ostendit etiam cum quanto gaudio hi qui tempore gratiæ exstiterunt, adventum Filii Dei susceperunt, et qualiter Ecclesia, plenitudine gentium intrante, sit aucta : quod nunc cernitur. Insinuat quoque qualiter tandem reliquiæ Israel salvæ fient : quod constat esse futurum. Iterum ait Anselmus : Materia hujus libri seu operis, est sponsus et sponsa, id est Christus et sancta Ecclesia tam adventum Christi præcedens, quam subsequens. Quamvis enim Patriarchæ et Prophetæ ceterique fideles ante adventum Christi existentes, dicti sunt fidelis Synagoga: tamen propter unitatem fidei, possunt et ipsi dici Ecclesia. Deinde post hæc Anselmus subjecit : De hac materia tam beata, ita agit hic Salomon, quod in primis ostendit quantopere sancti patres ante legem et sub lege exoptaverunt Christi adventum, et quam gratulanter susceperunt eumdem qui fuerunt tempore gratiæ.
paras.en: Moreover Anselm, Archbishop of Canterbury, in his prologue on the Canticles, wrote: This book is said to come under prophecy (which is made of the past, the present and the future), because it shows with how great desire the faithful Synagogue longed for and awaited the coming of Christ: which is now past. It shows also with how great joy those who lived in the time of grace received the coming of the Son of God, and how the Church grew as the fullness of the Gentiles came in: which is now seen. It intimates also how at last the [[Rom 9:27|remnant|reliquiæ]] of Israel [[Rom 9:27|shall be saved|salvæ fient]]: which is certain to come. Again Anselm says: The matter of this book or work is the bridegroom and the bride, that is, Christ and holy Church, both the Church that went before the coming of Christ and that which followed it. For although the Patriarchs and Prophets and the other faithful who lived before the coming of Christ are called the faithful Synagogue, yet, because of the unity of faith, they too can be called the Church. Then after this Anselm added: Of this so blessed matter Solomon here treats in such a way that he shows, first of all, how earnestly the holy fathers before the Law and under the Law longed for the coming of Christ, and how joyfully those who lived in the time of grace received Him.

paras.t: Amplius, S. Bernardus in exordio secundi sermonis super Cantica, loquitur : Ardorem desiderii patrum suspirantium Christi in carne præsentiam, frequentissime cogitans, compungor et confundor in memetipso, et nunc vix contineo lacrimas: ita tædet teporis torporisque miserabilium temporum horum. Cui namque nostrum tantum ingerit gaudium gratiæ hujus exhibitio, quantum Sanctis veteribus accenderat desiderium promissio? Et sicut consequenter docet Bernardus, in illorum patrum veteris Testamenti persona in exordio hujus dicitur libri, Osculetur me osculo oris sui, videlicet in persona Synagogæ, vel Ecclesiæ Synagogam comprehendentis. Subdit quippe Bernardus : Illorum ergo desiderium flagrans et piæ exspectationis affectum, sonat mihi vox illa, Osculetur me osculo oris sui.
paras.en: Further, St. Bernard, at the opening of his second sermon on the Canticles, says: Thinking very often of the ardent desire of the fathers who sighed for the presence of Christ in the flesh, I am pierced and confounded within myself, and even now I can scarcely hold back my tears: so weary am I of the lukewarmness and torpor of these wretched times. For to which of us does the showing forth of this grace bring as much joy as the promise of it had kindled desire in the saints of old? And, as Bernard goes on to teach, it is in the person of those fathers of the Old Testament that at the beginning of this book is said, [[1:1|Let him kiss me with the kiss of his mouth|Osculetur me osculo oris sui]]: that is, in the person of the Synagogue, or of the Church as it comprehends the Synagogue. For Bernard adds: Their burning desire, then, and the affection of their devout expectation, is what that voice sounds to me: [[1:1|Let him kiss me with the kiss of his mouth|Osculetur me osculo oris sui]].

paras.t: Præterea sanctus Gregorius circa exordium expositionis libri istius, apertissime dicit : Ponamus ante oculos omne genus humanum, ab exordio mundi usque ad finem ejus, totam videlicet Ecclesiam esse unam sponsam, quæ arrhas spirituali dono per legem perceperat; sed tamen sponsi sui præsentiam quærebat, quæ dicit : Osculetur me osculo oris sui.
paras.en: Moreover St. Gregory, near the beginning of his exposition of this book, says most plainly: Let us set before our eyes the whole human race, from the beginning of the world to its end, that is, the whole Church, as one bride, who had received a pledge [arrhas, the earnest given at a betrothal] in a spiritual gift through the Law, but yet sought the presence of her Bridegroom; she it is who says: [[1:1|Let him kiss me with the kiss of his mouth|Osculetur me osculo oris sui]].

paras.t: Ecce tot et tantorum Patrum catholicorum testimoniis elucescit, quod liber hic tractet de Christo atque Ecclesia : non prout Ecclesia contra Synagogam dividitur, sed prout Synagogam includit; et non Synagogam duntaxat, sed et Sanctos qui ab exordio mundi fuerunt, ante legem scriptam sub lege naturæ. Non ergo doctores catholici ab una parte ponendi sunt, tanquam nimis extremi, contra doctores Hebræos quasi ab alia parte nimis extremos: ita ut quis modernis temporibus se ponat quasi in medio inter illos, tanquam verum intellectum libri hujus præ omnibus illis introducturus. Nam et præallegatos doctores præcipuos secuti sunt expositores posteriores; nec recolo me in aliquo expositore catholico notabili et famoso legisse, quod liber iste loquatur de Ecclesia contra Synagogam distincta, et præcise de plebe christiana. Et dato quod aliqui, respectu præallegatorum parvæ aut nullius auctoritatis, hoc dicerent : ob hoc non esset indeterminate dicendum, quod expositores catholici dicant hoc.
paras.en: Behold, by the testimonies of so many and such great Catholic Fathers it is made clear that this book treats of Christ and the Church: not as the Church is set apart from the Synagogue, but as it includes the Synagogue; and not the Synagogue only, but also the saints who were from the beginning of the world, before the written Law, under the law of nature. The Catholic doctors, then, are not to be put on one side, as too extreme, over against the Hebrew doctors, as too extreme on the other side, so that someone in modern times should set himself as it were in the middle between them, as though he were to bring in the true understanding of this book before all of them. For the later expositors too followed the principal doctors cited above; nor do I remember reading in any notable and famous Catholic expositor that this book speaks of the Church as distinct from the Synagogue, and precisely of the Christian people. And granted that some, of little or no authority compared with those cited above, said this, it ought not on that account to be said without qualification that the Catholic expositors say it.

1.title: QUALES DEBEANT ESSE LECTORES ET AUDITORES LIBRI ISTIUS.
1.title_en: What manner of men the readers and hearers of this book ought to be

paras.t: Origenes in prologo suo super Cantica scribit : In verbis Cantici canticorum ille est cibus, de quo ait Apostolus : Perfectorum est solidus cibus. Si vero aliquis accesserit, qui secundum carnem tantummodo vir est, huic tali non parum ex hac Scriptura discriminis periculique nascetur. Audire enim pure et castis auribus amoris nomina nesciens, ab interiori homine ad exteriorem et carnalem virum, omnem deflectet auditum, et a spiritu convertetur ad carnem, nutrietque in semetipso concupiscentias carnis, et occasione divinæ Scripturæ, ad carnalem libidinem videbitur incitari. Ob hoc moneo et consilium do omni, qui nondum carnis et sanguinis caret molestiis, neque ab affectu naturæ materialis abscedit, ut a lectione libelli hujus, eorumque quæ in eo dicentur, penitus temperet. Aiunt enim observari etiam apud Hebræos, quod nisi quis ad ætatem perfectam maturamque pervenerit, libellum hunc nec in manibus quidem tenere permittatur. Sed et illud ab eis accepimus custodiri, quoniam quidem moris est apud eos, omnes Scripturas a doctoribus et sapientibus tradi pueris, similiter et eas quas δευτερώσεις appellant ; ad ultimum vero quatuor ista servari, principium Genesis, et primum capitulum Ezechielis, et finem ejus, scilicet visionem de ædificatione templi, atque hunc librum, scilicet librum hunc Cantici canticorum. Hæc Origenes. Cujus recitationi de hac Hebræorum consuetudine consonat, quod super Ezechielem refert Hieronymus, apud Hebræos nullum admitti ad prætactas quatuor partes Scripturarum veteris Testamenti, quousque tricesimum attigerit annum ætatis.
paras.en: Origen, in his prologue on the Canticles, writes: In the words of the Canticle of Canticles is that food of which the Apostle says: [[Heb 5:14|strong meat is for the perfect|Perfectorum est solidus cibus]]. But if anyone should come to it who is a man only according to the flesh, no small hazard and danger will arise for such a one from this Scripture. For, not knowing how to hear the names of love with pure and chaste ears, he will turn all his hearing away from the inward man to the outward and carnal man, and will be turned from the spirit to the flesh, and will nourish in himself the desires of the flesh, and will seem to be stirred up to carnal lust by occasion of the divine Scripture. For this reason I warn and counsel everyone who is not yet free of the troubles of flesh and blood, and has not withdrawn from the affection of material nature, to abstain altogether from reading this little book and the things that will be said on it. For they say it is observed even among the Hebrews that, unless one has reached a full and ripe age, he is not allowed even to hold this little book in his hands. And we have received from them that this too is kept: since it is their custom that all the Scriptures are handed on to the boys by the doctors and wise men, and likewise those which they call deuteroseis [δευτερώσεις, "second teachings": the Jewish traditions handed down beside the written Law], these four are kept back to the last: the beginning of Genesis, the first chapter of Ezechiel, and its end, that is, the vision of the building of the temple, and this book, that is, this book of the Canticle of Canticles. Thus far Origen. With his account of this custom of the Hebrews agrees what Jerome reports on Ezechiel: that among the Hebrews no one is admitted to the four parts of the Scriptures of the Old Testament just mentioned until he has reached the thirtieth year of his age.

paras.t: Præterea Gregorius in prooemio suo super Cantica loquitur : Nominantur in hoc libro oscula, ubera, genæ, et femora : in quibus verbis non irridenda est sacra Scriptura, sed misericordia Dei pensanda est, quam mirabiliter et misericorditer operetur nobiscum, qui ut cor nostrum ad investigationem sacri amoris accenderet, usque ad turpis amoris nostri verba descendit. Sed unde se loquendo humiliat, inde nos intellectu exaltat : quia ex sermonibus hujus amoris discimus, qua virtute in Deitatis amore ferveamus. Hoc autem nobis solerter intuendum est, ne quum verba exterioris amoris audimus, ad exteriora sentienda moveamur ; et machina quæ ponitur ut levet, ipsa magis opprimat ne levemur. Debemus ergo in verbis istis corporeis, quidquid interius est quærere, et loquendo de corpore, quasi extra corpus esse. Debemus ad has nuptias sponsi et sponsæ cum intellectu intimæ caritatis, id est cum veste nuptiali, venire, ne in tenebras ignorantiæ repellamur. Qui igitur librum hunc legit aut audit, nihil passibile aut sensuale habeat in corde, ut secundum interiorem hominem nova creatura sit. Sacra etenim hæc Scriptura mons est, quem si bestia tetigerit, lapidabitur. Bestia quippe tangit montem, quando irrationabilibus dediti motibus, celsitudini sacræ Scripturæ propinquant, et eam non secundum quod debent, pure spiritualiterque intelligunt, sed irrationabiliter ad suæ voluptatis intelligentiam flectunt.
paras.en: Moreover Gregory, in his preface on the Canticles, says: In this book kisses, breasts, cheeks and thighs are named; and in these words holy Scripture is not to be mocked, but the mercy of God is to be pondered: how wonderfully and mercifully He deals with us, who, to kindle our heart to the searching out of sacred love, came down even to the words of our shameful love. But by the very means by which He humbles Himself in speaking, He exalts us in understanding: for from the words of this love we learn with what strength we should burn in the love of the Godhead. But this we must carefully watch, lest, when we hear the words of outward love, we be moved to feel outward things, and the machine that is set up to lift us should itself rather weigh us down, so that we are not lifted. In these bodily words, therefore, we ought to seek whatever is within, and in speaking of the body be as it were outside the body. We ought to come to these nuptials of the Bridegroom and the bride with the understanding of inmost charity, that is, with the wedding garment, lest we be driven out into the darkness of ignorance[[Matt 22:12||]][[Matt 22:13||]]. Let him, then, who reads or hears this book have nothing passible [that is, subject to passion] or sensual in his heart, so that according to the inward man he may be a new creature. For this sacred Scripture is a mountain which, if [[Heb 12:20|a beast shall touch|bestia tetigerit]] it, [[Heb 12:20|it shall be stoned|lapidabitur]][[Ex 19:12||]][[Ex 19:13||]]. For a beast touches the mountain when men given up to irrational impulses draw near to the height of sacred Scripture, and do not understand it purely and spiritually, as they ought, but irrationally bend it to a sense that serves their own pleasure.

paras.t: Insuper Cancellarius Parisiensis, per quem in toto opusculo isto magistrum Joannem de Gerson doctissimum virum intelligo, in editione sua super Cantica fatur : Credulitatem secretissimorum sensuum et castissimorum affectuum, quos fumus literalis includit, nullus abhorreat, neque scandalum fœdæ carnalitatis incurrat. Puderet referre quid expertus audivi : offenderet enim pias aures.
paras.en: Further, the Chancellor of Paris (by whom, throughout this little work, I mean Master John Gerson, a most learned man), in his work on the Canticles, says: Let no one shrink from believing in the most secret meanings and most chaste affections which the smoke of the letter encloses, nor fall into the scandal of foul carnality. I should be ashamed to tell what I have heard from experience: for it would offend pious ears.

paras.t: Ecce tot prudentissimis et expertissimis testibus constat, quales oporteat esse lectores et auditores hujus libri, qui in superficie carnalissimus esse videtur, sed in vera intelligentia spiritualissimus comprobatur. Oportet, inquam, ut sint reformati atque a sensualibus affectibus depurati, ne vocabula ista rerum carnalium advertentes, carnalia imaginentur, sed mox ad intellectualia et spiritualia elevantur : alioqui intus lædentur.
paras.en: Behold, by so many most prudent and most experienced witnesses it is established what manner of readers and hearers this book ought to have, which on the surface seems most carnal, but in its true understanding is proved most spiritual. They must, I say, be reformed and cleansed of sensual affections, so that, when they attend to these words for carnal things, they do not imagine carnal things, but are at once lifted up to things intellectual and spiritual: otherwise they will be hurt within.

paras.t: Quid ergo agendum est multis religiosis atque canonicis et aliis in sacris Ordinibus, qui in ecclesia et divino Officio hæc audire seu legere habent, quum nondum sint taliter emundati, et sine fœda imaginatione in tali loco et hora vix legunt et audiunt ista, imo spiritualem et veram eorum intelligentiam vix attingunt? His arbitror consulendum, ut pro posse studeant librum hunc vere et pure intelligere, sicut oportet, vel saltem in generali cognoscant et pensent, omnia verba libri istius spiritualiter ac purissime esse intelligenda : sicque ad memoriam Dei, ad considerationem Domini nostri Jesu Christi, ac suæ Ecclesiæ et Virginis gloriosæ, mutuique eorum amoris mundissimi, elevent corda sua, meditando de talibus saltem in quodam communi, atque ab omni indecenti imaginatione mox abstrahant se.
paras.en: What, then, are the many religious and canons and others in sacred Orders to do, who have to hear or read these things in church and in the divine Office, when they are not yet so cleansed, and scarcely read and hear them in such a place and at such an hour without foul imaginings, nay, scarcely reach their spiritual and true understanding? These, I think, should be counselled to strive as far as they can to understand this book truly and purely, as is fitting, or at least to know and ponder in general that all the words of this book are to be understood spiritually and most purely; and so to lift up their hearts to the remembrance of God, to the consideration of our Lord Jesus Christ, and of His Church and of the glorious Virgin, and of their most pure love for one another, meditating on such things at least in a general way, and at once to withdraw themselves from every unbecoming imagining.

1.title: EXPOSITIO CAPITULI PRIMI : OSCULETUR ME OSCULO ORIS SUI : DE CHRISTO ET UNIVERSALI ECCLESIA.
1.title_en: Exposition of the first chapter: Let him kiss me with the kiss of his mouth: of Christ and the universal Church

paras.t: MULTIFARIE multisque modis Deus Pater, omnipotens, æternus, ab exordio mundi per verba et signa, per visiones, figuras, oracula, unigenitum suum Filium prædixit incarnandum, ac liberaturum genus humanum. Et hoc ipsum in lege naturæ ab Adam usque ad Moysen et legis scriptæ collationem, cognoverunt præcipui Patriarchæ et sancti viri, Adam, Seth, Enoch, Noe, Sem, Abraham, Isaac, Jacob, multique alii homines virtuosi, ex revelatione divina aut patrum suorum narratione : qui omnes Salvatoris adventum et Christi incarnationem, apparitionem, redemptionemque mundi ardentius optaverunt, quam æstimare valemus. Denique in monte Sinai revelata sunt desuper Moysi mysteria Christi, et qualiter de Christo facta fuit promissio illa, In semine tuo benedicentur omnes gentes, non solum Abrahæ, sed etiam Isaac et Jacob, prout in Genesi Moyses ipse descripsit. Postea vero sub lege per David, Salomonem, Isaiam, aliosque Prophetas prænuntiata et descripta sunt mysteria Salvatoris multo diffusius, quam sub lege naturæ : ita quod Judæi sub lege Moysis communiter crediderunt explicite, Salvatorem generis humani venturum in mundum. Quod totum constat ex eo, quod Christus in Evangelio suis ait discipulis : Beati oculi qui vident quæ vos videtis. Dico enim vobis, quod multi reges et Prophetæ et justi voluerunt videre quæ vos videtis, et non viderunt, et audire quæ auditis, et non audierunt.
paras.en: [[Heb 1:1|At sundry times and in divers manners|MULTIFARIE multisque modis]] God the Father, almighty and eternal, from the beginning of the world foretold, by words and signs, by visions, figures and oracles, that His only-begotten Son would become incarnate and would set mankind free. And this very thing was known under the law of nature, from Adam until Moses and the giving of the written law, to the chief Patriarchs and holy men, Adam, Seth, Enoch, Noe, Sem, Abraham, Isaac, Jacob, and many other virtuous men, by divine revelation or by what their fathers told them: and all of them longed for the coming of the Saviour, and for the incarnation of Christ, His appearing and the redemption of the world, more ardently than we are able to reckon. Then on Mount Sinai the mysteries of Christ were revealed from on high to Moses, and how that promise, [[Gen 22:18|in thy seed shall all the nations|In semine tuo]] [[Gen 22:18|be blessed|benedicentur omnes gentes]][[Gen 26:4||]][[Gen 28:14||]], was made concerning Christ, not to Abraham only but also to Isaac and Jacob, as Moses himself described in Genesis. Afterwards, under the law, the mysteries of the Saviour were foretold and described far more fully through David, Solomon, Isaias and the other Prophets than under the law of nature: so that the Jews under the law of Moses commonly believed explicitly that the Saviour of mankind would come into the world. All of which is plain from this, that Christ says to His disciples in the Gospel: [[Luke 10:23|Blessed are the eyes that see the things which you see|Beati oculi qui vident quæ vos videtis]]. [[Luke 10:24|For I say to you that many prophets and kings have desired to see the things that you see and have not seen them; and to hear the things that you hear and have not heard them|Dico enim vobis, quod multi reges et Prophetæ et justi voluerunt videre quæ vos videtis, et non viderunt, et audire quæ auditis, et non audierunt]] [Denis reads "many kings and prophets and just men"].

paras.t: Itaque in persona universorum illorum fidelium, qui sub lege naturæ legeque scripta fuerunt, et Christi adventum ardentissime cupierunt, nunc dicitur : Osculetur me osculo oris sui : id est, Salvator mundi, Filius Dei, mihi tam diu totiesque promissus, per incarnationis mysterium personaliter veniat, naturam meam in unitate personæ assumat, se ipsum mihi facie ad faciem repræsentet, ore ad os mihi loquatur, inter homines conversetur : sicque in medio terræ meam operetur salutem. Denique, quam æstuanter Sancti antiqui istud desideraverunt, perpendere possumus : Primo ex dignitate et excellentia sponsi istius, cujus nobilitas est immensa, speciositas infinita, sapientia prorsus interminabilis, opulentia illimitabilis, incircumscripta suavitas, supercopiosissima pietas, et beatitudo sine termino et mensura. Non itaque mirum, si tali ac tanto tam infinitæ excellentiæ atque dulcedinis sponso, optavit uniri et desponsari hæc sponsa. Secundo id ipsum perpendere possumus ex magnitudine indigentiæ sponsæ istius. Erat namque damnata exsilio, ejecta de paradiso, jugo peccati gravata, servituti ac potestati diaboli aliquo modo subjecta, atque æternæ beatitudinis jucunditatibus destituta ; in lacum miseriæ lutumque fœcis erat projecta, nec erat qui manum porrigeret adjutricem, per subventionem completam et redemptionem finalem. Tertio idem pensare valemus ex miro, copioso et saluberrimo fructu, qui provenit Ecclesiæ ex prætacto osculo sponsi istius : quia per ipsum a cunctis malis præinductis est liberata, ad sanctam libertatem reducta, amica, sponsa, filia, hæres, consors sui Creatoris effecta, charismatibus gratiarum mirifice decorata. Per ipsum facta est gens sancta, populus acquisitionis, genus electum, regale sacerdotium, præ cunctis nationibus gloriosa.
paras.en: And so, in the person of all those faithful who lived under the law of nature and under the written law, and who most ardently longed for the coming of Christ, it is now said: [[1:1|Let him kiss me with the kiss of his mouth|Osculetur me osculo oris sui]]: that is, may the Saviour of the world, the Son of God, so long and so often promised to me, come in person through the mystery of the incarnation; may He take up my nature into the unity of His person, show Himself to me face to face, speak to me mouth to mouth, and dwell among men: and so work my salvation in the midst of the earth[[Ps 73:12||]] [the margin gives Ps. lxxxiii, 12; the words are from Ps 73:12, "he hath wrought salvation in the midst of the earth"]. Now how burningly the holy men of old desired this, we can weigh: First, from the dignity and excellence of this Bridegroom, whose nobility is immeasurable, His beauty infinite, His wisdom altogether without bound, His riches without limit, His sweetness uncircumscribed, His goodness superabundant, and His beatitude without end or measure. It is no wonder, then, if this bride longed to be united and espoused to such and so great a Bridegroom, of so infinite an excellence and sweetness. Secondly, we can weigh the same from the greatness of this bride's need. For she was condemned to exile, cast out of paradise, weighed down by the yoke of sin, in some manner subject to the servitude and power of the devil, and stripped of the delights of eternal beatitude; she had been thrown into [[Ps 39:3|the pit of misery and the mire of dregs|lacum miseriæ lutumque fœcis]], and there was none to stretch out a helping hand by a full relief and a final redemption. Thirdly, we can consider the same from the wonderful, abundant and most wholesome fruit that came to the Church from the aforesaid kiss of this Bridegroom: for by it she was set free from all the evils brought upon her before, led back to holy liberty, made the friend, the bride, the daughter, the heir and the partner of her Creator, and wonderfully adorned with the gifts of graces. By it she was made [[1 Pet 2:9|a holy nation, a purchased people|gens sancta, populus acquisitionis]], [[1 Pet 2:9|a chosen generation, a kingly priesthood|genus electum, regale sacerdotium]], glorious above all nations.

paras.t: Præterea, sicut in sponso isto, Domino Jesu Christo, est duplex natura, divina videlicet et humana, ita et duplex os, puta divinum et increatum, humanumque et creatum. Os Christi divinum et increatum, est intellectus seu sapientia ejus æterna, per quam loquitur omni menti bene dispositæ, juxta illud Psalmistæ : Audiam quid loquatur in me Dominus Deus. In Job quoque legitur : Semel loquitur Deus, et secundo id ipsum non repetit. Unde quibusdam improperat per Prophetam, dicentem : Væ, filii desertores, ut faceretis consilium, et non ex me, et os meum non interrogastis. Amplius, hoc increato ore suo loquitur Unigenitus Dei universis Beatis in patria immediate ea, quæ ad essentiale præmium pertinent eorumdem. Nempe hæc locutio non est nisi manifestatio qua eis ostendit clare se ipsum, seu divinam essentiam, ad intuendum ac perfruendum. Estque locutio ista toti supergloriosissimæ Trinitati communis, quemadmodum et idem numero intellectus est in tribus adorandis superdignissimisque Personis. Actiones etenim Dei ad extra, communes sunt summæ et individuæ Trinitati. De effectibus autem suis loquitur Verbum æternum quædam immediate superioribus angelicis mentibus, per quas et inferiores angelicas illuminat mentes de talibus; et per sanctos angelos loquitur inde hominibus : prout in libris de Angelica et Ecclesiastica hierarchiis docet Dionysius Magnus.
paras.en: Moreover, as in this Bridegroom, the Lord Jesus Christ, there is a twofold nature, namely divine and human, so there is also a twofold mouth, divine and uncreated, and human and created. The divine and uncreated mouth of Christ is His eternal understanding or wisdom, by which He speaks to every well-disposed mind, according to that word of the Psalmist: [[Ps 84:9|I will hear what the Lord God will speak in me|Audiam quid loquatur in me Dominus Deus]]. In Job too we read: [[Job 33:14|God speaketh once, and repeateth not the selfsame thing the second time|Semel loquitur Deus, et secundo id ipsum non repetit]]. Hence He reproaches certain men through the Prophet, who says: [[Is 30:1|Woe to you, apostate children|Væ, filii desertores]], [[Is 30:1|that you would take counsel, and not of me|ut faceretis consilium, et non ex me]], and [[Is 30:2|have not asked at my mouth|os meum non interrogastis]]. Further, with this uncreated mouth of His the Only-begotten of God speaks immediately to all the Blessed in the fatherland the things that belong to their essential reward [that is, the vision of God itself, as distinct from the accidental joys added to it]. For this speaking is nothing other than the manifestation by which He shows Himself, that is, the divine essence, clearly to them, to behold and to enjoy. And this speaking is common to the whole most supremely glorious Trinity, just as the understanding is one and the same in number in the three adorable and most supremely worthy Persons. For the works of God outside Himself are common to the supreme and undivided Trinity. But concerning His effects the eternal Word speaks certain things immediately to the higher angelic minds, through which He also enlightens the lower angelic minds about such things; and through the holy angels He then speaks to men: as Dionysius the Great teaches in the books On the Angelic and the Ecclesiastical Hierarchies.

paras.t: Itaque, dum Verbum æternum, Unigenitus Dei, sibi ipsi conjunxit naturam humanam hypostatica unione, assumendo eam ad suum esse personale æternum et increatum, tunc immediate tetigit, circumplexus et osculatus est eam, et per eam osculatus est omnes nos. Propter quod ad Hebræos scribit Apostolus : Nusquam angelos apprehendit, sed semen Abrahæ apprehendit. Deinde visus in terris, et cum hominibus conversatus, osculatus est nos, per se ipsum alloquendo, instruendo, consolando fideles, eosque Deo Patri reconciliando. Denique discipulos suos ad se redeuntes consuevit in osculo sancto etiam corporali recipere. Unde per Zachariam prophetam prædixit: Gaude et lætare, filia Sion, quia ecce ego venio, et habitabo in medio tui; et applicabuntur gentes multæ ad Dominum in die illa. Hinc etiam in alio Propheta fuit prædictum: Qui fecit stellas, hic est Deus noster; hic adinvenit omnem viam disciplinæ, et dedit illam Jacob puero suo, et Israel dilecto suo. Post hæc in terris visus est, et cum hominibus conversatus est.
paras.en: And so, when the eternal Word, the Only-begotten of God, joined human nature to Himself by the hypostatic union [that is, the union of the two natures in the one Person of the Word], taking it up into His own eternal and uncreated personal being, He then touched it immediately, embraced it and kissed it, and through it He kissed all of us. For this reason the Apostle writes to the Hebrews: [[Heb 2:16|nowhere doth he take hold of the angels: but of the seed of Abraham he taketh hold|Nusquam angelos apprehendit, sed semen Abrahæ apprehendit]]. Then, seen upon earth and conversing with men[[Bar 3:38||]], He kissed us, by speaking to the faithful Himself, instructing and consoling them, and reconciling them to God the Father. And He was accustomed to receive His disciples, when they came back to Him, with a holy kiss, even a bodily one. Hence He foretold through the prophet Zacharias: [[Zach 2:10|Sing praise, and rejoice, O daughter of Sion: for behold I come, and I will dwell in the midst of thee|Gaude et lætare, filia Sion, quia ecce ego venio, et habitabo in medio tui]] [Denis reads Gaude, "rejoice", for "sing praise"]; [[Zach 2:11|And many nations shall be joined to the Lord in that day|et applicabuntur gentes multæ ad Dominum in die illa]]. Hence it was also foretold in another Prophet: He that made the stars[[Bar 3:35||]], [[Bar 3:36|This is our God|hic est Deus noster]]; [[Bar 3:37|He found out all the way of knowledge, and gave it to Jacob his servant, and to Israel his beloved|hic adinvenit omnem viam disciplinæ, et dedit illam Jacob puero suo, et Israel dilecto suo]]. [[Bar 3:38|Afterwards he was seen upon earth, and conversed with men|Post hæc in terris visus est, et cum hominibus conversatus est]]

paras.t: Quæri etiam potest, qualiter Ecclesia humilis, ausa fuit tantæ majestatis sponsi osculum flagitare, cui exercitus cœli cum tremore adsistit, quem Cherubim Seraphimque adorant; de quo in Job legitur: Magnus fortitudine, et judicio, et justitia; et enarrari non potest: ideo timebunt eum viri, et non audebunt contemplari omnes qui videntur sibi esse sapientes. Ad quod breviter respondendum, quod duo specialiter incitaverunt Ecclesiam ad postulandum nuptiale hoc osculum. Primum, quoniam ipse benignissimus sponsus tam gratiose eam prævenit, suam incarnationem et adventum ei prænuntiando ac promittendo: et ex hoc ipsa concepit fiduciam id petendi. Secundum fuit ardentissima caritas Ecclesiæ ad hunc sponsum. Caritas autem, separationis impatiens est, unionisque avida, et frequenter prædominando rationem transcendit; et ingerit se dilecto, quem quanto æstuantius amat, tanto propinquius, imo et intimius appetit ei uniri: ac grandem parit fiduciam, respicitque dilectum potius ut dilectum, quam ut dominum aut majorem. Potest addi et tertium, videlicet magnitudo necessitatis, quæ lege non stringitur. Indiguit enim vehementissime salvatore, nec salvari potuit nisi per istiusmodi sponsum.
paras.en: It may also be asked how the lowly Church dared to beg for the kiss of a Bridegroom of such majesty, before whom the host of heaven stands with trembling, whom the Cherubim and Seraphim adore; of whom we read in Job: [[Job 37:23|great in strength, and in judgment, and in justice, and he is ineffable|Magnus fortitudine, et judicio, et justitia; et enarrari non potest]]: [[Job 37:24|Therefore men shall fear him, and all that seem to themselves to be wise, shall not dare to behold him|ideo timebunt eum viri, et non audebunt contemplari omnes qui videntur sibi esse sapientes]]. To this the short answer is that two things in particular moved the Church to ask for this nuptial kiss. The first, that this most kind Bridegroom Himself so graciously went before her, foretelling and promising her His incarnation and coming: and from this she conceived the confidence to ask for it. The second was the Church's most ardent charity towards this Bridegroom. Now charity cannot bear separation and is eager for union, and often, prevailing, it goes beyond reason; and it presses itself upon the beloved, and the more burningly it loves him, the more closely, nay the more intimately, it longs to be united to him: and it begets great confidence, and looks upon the beloved rather as beloved than as lord or superior. A third may be added, namely the greatness of her need, which is bound by no law. For she needed a saviour most urgently, and could not be saved except through such a Bridegroom.

paras.t: Consequenter sponsa hæc, universalis Ecclesia, causam aperit suæ petitionis, et a tertia persona convertitur ad secundam, et eum jam alloquitur quasi præsentem, dicendo: quia meliora sunt ubera tua vino: de quo, tanquam de absente, præmisit, Osculetur me osculo oris sui. Quæ enim suspiriose cupit cœlestis sponsi præsentiam, eo ipso quo sic ad ipsum afficitur, aliqualem ejus præsentiam mox meretur: siquidem prope est Dominus omnibus invocantibus eum, omnibus invocantibus eum in veritate. Noverat quoque hæc sponsa sponsum suum, nec loco, nec tempore circumscribi, sed esse ubique præsentem.
paras.en: Next this bride, the universal Church, discloses the reason for her petition, and turns from the third person to the second, and now addresses Him as though present, saying: [[1:1|for thy breasts are better than wine|quia meliora sunt ubera tua vino]]: Him of whom, as of one absent, she had said before, [[1:1|Let him kiss me with the kiss of his mouth|Osculetur me osculo oris sui]]. For she who longs with sighs for the presence of the heavenly Bridegroom, by the very fact that she is so moved towards Him, soon merits some presence of His: since [[Ps 144:18|The Lord is nigh unto all them that call upon him: to all that call upon him in truth|prope est Dominus omnibus invocantibus eum, omnibus invocantibus eum in veritate]]. This bride knew, too, that her Bridegroom is not circumscribed by place or by time, but is present everywhere.

paras.t: Ideo ut præsentem confidenter alloquitur: et quæ quasi orando dixit ad Patrem sponsi sui æternum, Osculetur me osculo oris sui, o Pater æterne, Unigenitus tuus; mox sponsi amore plus quam ante succensa, non quivit diutius ab ejus alloquio abstinere. Nempe qui ardentissime amat, sui sermonis variat modum ac ordinem, secundum diversum sui amoris impulsum ac tactum et flammam. Ideo super Cantica asserit Alexander: Modum sui sermonis non continet amor, directo tenore non graditur.
paras.en: Therefore she addresses Him confidently as present: and she who, as though in prayer, had said to the eternal Father of her Bridegroom, [[1:1|Let him kiss me with the kiss of his mouth|Osculetur me osculo oris sui]], that is, O eternal Father, let Thy Only-begotten do so, soon, kindled with love of the Bridegroom more than before, could no longer keep from speaking to Him. For one who loves most ardently varies the manner and order of his speech according to the varying impulse, touch and flame of his love. Hence Alexander says on the Canticles: Love does not keep to one manner of speech; it does not walk on a straight course.

paras.t: Itaque ait: Meliora sunt ubera tua vino. Per ubera sponsi, secundum Origenem, intelliguntur arcana cordis seu pectoris Christi, hoc est thesauri sapientiæ et scientiæ in ipso absconditi, quibus alit suorum corda fidelium. Possunt quoque per duo ubera sponsi, intelligi duo caritatis præcepta; item vetus Testamentum spiritualiter intellectum, ac novum; et rursus præcepta Salvatoris, et evangelica ejus consilia; similiter misericordia ejus et veritas; itemque gratia præveniens, et subsequens. Hæc ubera meliora sunt vino, id est doctrina legis ac Prophetarum, et rigore contento in lege, litteralique sensu ipsius, atque cærimonialibus ac judicialibus legis præceptis. Magna equidem est eminentia evangelicæ legis, quæ est lex caritatis, et gratiam continens ac conferens, et opere exhibens quod prædicebatur ac promittebatur in lege atque Prophetis, super ipsam legem, quæ fuit lex timoris, nec gratiam continebat, ac nihil ad perfectum adduxit. Ideo in Evangelio Joannis scribitur: Lex per Moysen data est; gratia et veritas per Jesum Christum facta est. Propter quod tempus evangelicæ legis, tempus gratiæ nuncupatur.
paras.en: And so she says: [[1:1|thy breasts are better than wine|Meliora sunt ubera tua vino]]. By the Bridegroom's breasts, according to Origen, are understood the secrets of the heart or breast of Christ, that is, the treasures of wisdom and knowledge hidden in Him, with which He feeds the hearts of His faithful. By the two breasts of the Bridegroom may also be understood the two precepts of charity; likewise the Old Testament spiritually understood, and the New; and again the precepts of the Saviour and His evangelical counsels; similarly His mercy and truth; and likewise prevenient and subsequent grace [that is, the grace that goes before the will and moves it, and the grace that accompanies and follows its consent]. These [[1:1|breasts are better than wine|ubera meliora sunt vino]], that is, than the teaching of the law and the Prophets, than the rigour contained in the law and its literal sense, and than the ceremonial and judicial precepts of the law. Great indeed is the pre-eminence of the law of the Gospel, which is the law of charity, containing and conferring grace, and showing in deed what was foretold and promised in the law and the Prophets, over the law itself, which was the law of fear, did not contain grace, and [[Heb 7:19|brought nothing to perfection|nihil ad perfectum adduxit]]. Therefore it is written in the Gospel of John: [[John 1:17|the law was given by Moses: grace and truth came by Jesus Christ|Lex per Moysen data est; gratia et veritas per Jesum Christum facta est]]. For this reason the time of the law of the Gospel is called the time of grace.

paras.t: Fragrantia unguentis optimis, id est pretiosissimis charismatibus gratiæ ac virtutum, ac sacro septenario Spiritus Sancti : quibus Christus secundum naturam assumptam fuit excellentissime inunctus, repletus et fragrans, sicut per Isaiam testatur : Spiritus Domini super me, eo quod unxerit me. Cui cantamus in Psalmo : Unxit te Deus, Deus tuus, oleo lætitiæ præ participibus tuis. De quo in Actibus Apostolorum sacratissimus princeps Apostolorum fatetur : Unxit eum Deus Spiritu Sancto et virtute. Insuper ubera Christi, id est documenta, præcepta, et evangelica ejus consilia, fragrant optimis unguentis, id est ecclesiasticis sacramentis : quæ sunt medicinalia vasa gratiarum cœlestium contentiva, quibus præceptorum violationes curantur, et quorum auxilio ipsa præcepta atque consilia prompto animo adimplentur : quæ optima unguenta ex fonte pectoris sponsi fluxerunt, imo et ex ejus latere in cruce perforato emanasse dicuntur.
paras.en: [[1:2|Smelling sweet of the best ointments|Fragrantia unguentis optimis]], that is, of the most precious gifts of grace and of the virtues, and of the sacred sevenfold gift of the Holy Ghost: with which Christ, according to the nature He assumed, was most excellently anointed, filled and fragrant, as He testifies through Isaias: [[Is 61:1|The spirit of the Lord is upon me, because the Lord hath anointed me|Spiritus Domini super me, eo quod unxerit me]] [Denis omits "the Lord" before "hath anointed"]. To whom we sing in the Psalm: [[Ps 44:8|God, thy God, hath anointed thee with the oil of gladness above thy fellows|Unxit te Deus, Deus tuus, oleo lætitiæ præ participibus tuis]]. Of whom the most holy prince of the Apostles declares in the Acts of the Apostles: [[Acts 10:38|God anointed him with the Holy Ghost and with power|Unxit eum Deus Spiritu Sancto et virtute]]. Moreover, the breasts of Christ, that is, His teachings, precepts and evangelical counsels, smell sweet of the best ointments, that is, of the sacraments of the Church: which are healing vessels containing heavenly graces, by which violations of the precepts are cured, and by whose help the precepts and counsels themselves are fulfilled with a ready mind: and these best ointments flowed from the fountain of the Bridegroom's breast, nay, they are said to have streamed from His side pierced on the cross.

paras.t: Circa hunc locum scribit quidam specialiter super illud, Quia meliora sunt ubera tua vino : In Hebræo habetur, Quia meliores sunt amores tui. Nomen enim Hebraicum hic positum, est æquivocum ad amores et ad ubera. Hebræi sequuntur unam significationem, translatio nostra aliam. Sed in hoc Hebræi videntur melius dicere, quia secundum proprietatem Hebraici sermonis, sponsa hic alloquitur sponsum. In commendatione autem sponsi, non videtur convenienter mentio fieri de uberibus. Est igitur sensus secundum Hebræos, quod amores sponsi sunt sapidiores menti devotæ, quam quodcumque sapidum corporale gustui corporali. — Circa hæc reor dicendum, quia si nomen illud Hebraicum est ad utrumque istud æquivocum, non potius habetur in Hebræo, Amores, quam, Ubera. Insuper videtur dicendum, quod Hieronymus aptius transtulit Ubera, ad insinuandum quod spiritualis sit intellectus, non sensus carnalis. Spiritualia etenim ubera, magis conveniunt sponso quam sponsæ, imo et uberibus sui alitur sponsi : et istud Cassiodorus tangit. Amplius Occam allegat Augustinum dicentem, quod viris proprie conveniunt mamillæ, feminis mammæ, pecoribus ubera : imo ubera pro mamillis et mammis accipi solent : sicque asserit Hugo, quod ubera data sunt viris in corporis ornamentum, non ad necessitatem. Ergo et ubera proprie competunt sponso : et certe sponsa in sponso libenter commemorat quod ipsa in se ipsa esse cognoscit, quatenus ex amborum similitudine, amor validius accendatur.
paras.en: On this place someone writes, specially on the words [[1:1|for thy breasts are better than wine|Quia meliora sunt ubera tua vino]]: In the Hebrew it reads, For thy loves are better. For the Hebrew word set here is ambiguous between "loves" and "breasts" [the Hebrew dodim, "loves", and dadim, "breasts", are written with the same letters]. The Hebrews follow one meaning, our translation the other. But in this the Hebrews seem to say it better, since according to the idiom of the Hebrew tongue the bride is here addressing the Bridegroom, and in praising a bridegroom it does not seem fitting to mention breasts. So the sense according to the Hebrews is that the Bridegroom's loves are more savoury to the devout mind than anything savoury in the body is to the bodily taste. On this I think it must be said that, if that Hebrew word is ambiguous between the two, the Hebrew no more reads "loves" than "breasts". Further it seems right to say that Jerome more fittingly translated "breasts", to suggest that the understanding is spiritual, not a carnal sense. For spiritual breasts belong to the Bridegroom more than to the bride, nay she herself is fed at the breasts of her Bridegroom: and Cassiodorus touches on this. Moreover Occam cites Augustine as saying that mamillæ properly belong to men, mammæ to women, and ubera to cattle [three Latin words for breasts or teats, which English cannot tell apart]: yet ubera are commonly taken for both mamillæ and mammæ: and so Hugh says that breasts were given to men as an ornament of the body, not for need. Therefore breasts too properly befit the Bridegroom: and surely the bride gladly recalls in the Bridegroom what she knows to be in herself, so that from the likeness of the two, love may be kindled the more strongly.

paras.t: Denique adhuc sponsi laudibus immoratur, et cur ejus osculum cupiat reserans, protestatur : Oleum effusum nomen tuum : id est, non solum tu ipse, o sponse, instar olei fusi, suavis et splendidus es; sed et nomen tuum, quodcumque sit illud, dulciter resonat in auribus meis, et ex sola nuncupatione tua dulcescit anima mea, reficitur, exhilaratur, clarescit. Insuper nomen tuum, id est fama excellentiæ tuæ toto orbe terrarum diffusa, fulget ac redolet, estque bonus odor Dei Patris, imo totius superpræstantissimæ Trinitatis in omni loco : sed et prædicatio majestatis tuæ coruscat, suaviterque odorat ut oleum vase fusum; et sicut oleum ceteris humoribus supernatat, sic nomen tuum præeminet universis. Quemadmodum etiam oleum ceteris cibis fert condimentum, influitque saporem, sic nomen tuum condimentum est Scripturarum, et spiritualibus eduliis animarum confert suavitatem. Rursus, sicut oleum lenit dolores ac vulnera sanat, sic nomen tuum, o sponse cœlestis, fugat a corde mœrorem, et vitiorum læsioni medetur.
paras.en: Then she lingers still on the praises of the Bridegroom, and, disclosing why she desires His kiss, declares: [[1:2|Thy name is as oil poured out|Oleum effusum nomen tuum]]: that is, not only art Thou Thyself, O Bridegroom, sweet and shining like oil poured out; but Thy name too, whatever it be, sounds sweetly in my ears, and at the mere naming of Thee my soul grows sweet, is refreshed, gladdened and brightened. Moreover Thy name, that is, the fame of Thy excellence spread through the whole world, shines and gives forth its fragrance, and is the good odour of God the Father, nay of the whole most supremely excellent Trinity, in every place[[2 Cor 2:15||]] ["in every place" is from the verse before, 2 Cor 2:14]: and the preaching of Thy majesty glitters, and smells sweet like oil poured from a vessel; and as oil floats above all other liquids, so Thy name stands above all things. And as oil gives seasoning to other foods and imparts flavour, so Thy name is the seasoning of the Scriptures, and lends sweetness to the spiritual food of souls. Again, as oil soothes pains and heals wounds, so Thy name, O heavenly Bridegroom, drives grief from the heart and heals the hurt of vices.

paras.t: De salubritate nominis hujus, angelus sanctus dixit ad Joseph : Vocabis nomen ejus Jesum; ipse enim salvum faciet populum suum a peccatis eorum. Siquidem Jesus interpretatur salvator : qui in Isaia sic effatur : Deus justus et salvans non est præter me. Atque in alio Propheta : Ego Dominus Deus tuus; et salvator non est præter me. Etenim Domino Jesu Christo secundum suam deitatem convenit salvare, propria et increata auctoritate et potestate : cui ex divina natura convenit peccata dimittere, dona gratiarum per creationem infundere, beatitudinemque æternam largiri. Porro secundum assumptam humanitatem, convenit ei salvare, ut causæ instrumentali, meritoriæ, eminenti, et tanquam mediatori ac satisfactori. Nam sicut corpus nostrum comparatur ad animam nostram, ut animæ instrumentum conjunctum, animatum, et proprium : sic humanitas Christi comparatur ad ejus deitatem et ad Verbum æternum quod eam assumpsit, velut instrumentum ipsius deitatis ac Verbi immediatum, conjunctum, animatum, et proprium : ut asserit Damascenus. Insuper, quam singulare, salubre et efficax sit nomen sponsi istius, pandit princeps Apostolorum, sic dicens : Nec enim aliud nomen sub cœlo datum est hominibus, in quo oporteat nos salvos fieri. De cujus nominis majestate Vas ait electionis : Dedit ei Deus Pater nomen, quod est super omne nomen, ut in nomine Jesu omne genu flectatur cœlestium, terrestrium, et infernorum.
paras.en: Of the saving power of this name the holy angel said to Joseph: [[Matt 1:21|thou shalt call his name Jesus. For he shall save his people from their sins|Vocabis nomen ejus Jesum; ipse enim salvum faciet populum suum a peccatis eorum]]. For Jesus means Saviour: who speaks thus in Isaias: [[Is 45:21|A just God and a saviour, there is none besides me|Deus justus et salvans non est præter me]]. And in another Prophet: [[Osee 13:4|I am the Lord thy God|Ego Dominus Deus tuus]]; [[Osee 13:4|and there is no saviour beside me|et salvator non est præter me]]. For to the Lord Jesus Christ according to His Godhead it belongs to save by His own uncreated authority and power: to whom, from the divine nature, it belongs to forgive sins, to pour in the gifts of graces by creation, and to bestow eternal beatitude. But according to the humanity He assumed, it belongs to Him to save as an instrumental, meritorious and pre-eminent cause, and as mediator and the one who makes satisfaction. For as our body is related to our soul as the soul's conjoined, living and proper instrument, so the humanity of Christ is related to His Godhead and to the eternal Word who assumed it, as the immediate, conjoined, living and proper instrument of that Godhead and Word: as Damascene says. Further, how singular, saving and effective the name of this Bridegroom is, the prince of the Apostles makes plain, saying: [[Acts 4:12|there is no other name under heaven given to men, whereby we must be saved|Nec enim aliud nomen sub cœlo datum est hominibus, in quo oporteat nos salvos fieri]]. Of the majesty of this name the Vessel of election [that is, St Paul, so called in Acts 9:15] says: God the Father [[Phil 2:9|hath given him a name which is above all names|Dedit ei Deus Pater nomen, quod est super omne nomen]], [[Phil 2:10|That in the name of Jesus every knee should bow, of those that are in heaven, on earth, and under the earth|ut in nomine Jesu omne genu flectatur cœlestium, terrestrium, et infernorum]].

paras.t: Præterea, Oleum effusum nomen tuum: id est, tu ipse, o illustrissime sponse, oleo compararis, et bonitas tua omni oleo exstat suavior, nobilitas tua omni oleo invenitur splendidior, unctio tua reficit mentes, pietas tua medetur animarum corporumque vulneribus, consolatio tua lenit pœnitentialem mærorem, et omnem inordinatam fugat tristitiam; ideo adolescentulæ dilexerunt te, id est particulares Ecclesiæ, et animæ spiritualiter renovatæ, atque incipientium mentes, et gentes olim paganæ, superbæ, carnales, inverecundæ, sed per gratiam tuam conversæ, et sobriæ, pudicæ, humilesque effectæ. Ad litteram quoque virgines sacræ, electæ puellæ, virtuosæ juvenculæ : quarum multæ pro tuo amore non solum totius mundi divitias, oblectamenta, honores, omnemque externum ornatum, vanitatem ac levitatem feminineam contempserunt; sed et crudelissima mortis genera virilissime pertulerunt, ac felicissime triumpharunt : quemadmodum sacratissima Catharina, præclarissima Ursula, et eis consimiles. Aliæ demum innumerabiles, in virginitate mentis ac corporis tibi constantissime servierunt ; et usque in præsens quasi innumeræ tales, in adolescentia sua relinquentes hoc sæculum nequam cum omni ejus fallacia, ingrediuntur cœnobia et reclusoria sancta, in quibus perpetuo clausæ manentes, tuis castissimis in spiritu vacant amplexibus.
paras.en: Again, [[1:2|Thy name is as oil poured out|Oleum effusum nomen tuum]]: that is, Thou Thyself, O most illustrious Bridegroom, art likened to oil, and Thy goodness is sweeter than any oil, Thy nobility is found brighter than any oil, Thy anointing refreshes minds, Thy loving-kindness heals the wounds of souls and bodies, Thy consolation soothes the grief of penance and drives away all disordered sadness; [[1:2|therefore young maidens have loved thee|ideo adolescentulæ dilexerunt te]], that is, the particular Churches, and souls spiritually renewed, and the minds of beginners, and the nations once pagan, proud, carnal and shameless, but converted by Thy grace and made sober, chaste and humble. Literally also, sacred virgins, chosen maidens, virtuous young women: many of whom, for love of Thee, not only despised the riches, delights and honours of the whole world, and all outward adornment, and womanly vanity and lightness, but also bore the cruellest kinds of death most manfully, and triumphed most happily: like the most holy Catharine, the most illustrious Ursula, and others like them. Others again without number have served Thee most constantly in virginity of mind and body; and to this day such women, almost without number, leaving in their youth this wicked world with all its deceit, enter convents and holy anchorholds, in which, remaining enclosed for ever, they give themselves to Thy most chaste embraces in the spirit.

paras.t: Trahe me post te. Istud in persona Ecclesiæ sub evangelica lege viventis, proprie sumitur : quæ sciens suum sponsum venisse, humanæ redemptionis mysteria complexisse, et ascendisse in cœlos, appetit sequi eum; sed recolens sponsum suum dixisse. Sine me nihil potestis facere, invocat gratiosum ejus auxilium, dicens : Trahe me post te, id est, excita et tolle meum torporem, accende in me tuæ caritatis ardorem, qui jugiter trahit sursum, quemadmodum ignis levatur in altum ; tuæ increatæ atque immensæ suavitatis sapore me affice, ut ad te solum pure jugiterque afficiar, tibi semper adhæream, ad te indesinenter adspirem : quatenus illam sancti tui Apostoli exhortationem adimpleam : Quæ sursum sunt quærite, ubi Christus est in dextera Dei sedens; quæ sursum sunt sapite, non quæ super terram. Scio enim te, Domine Jesu, dixisse : Si exaltatus fuero a terra, omnia traham ad me ipsum : et rursum. Nemo potest venire ad me, nisi Pater, qui misit me, traxerit eum. Nec dubito quin Deus Pater tuus, et tu Unigenitus ejus, sitis unus tractor, sicut et unus creator. Rursus, novi vere ab Apostolo dictum : Non sumus sufficientes cogitare aliquid ex nobis, quasi ex nobis: sed sufficientia nostra ex Deo est.
paras.en: [[1:3|Draw me|Trahe me]] [[1:3|after thee|post te]]. This is properly taken in the person of the Church living under the law of the Gospel: knowing that her Bridegroom has come, has fulfilled the mysteries of man's redemption and has ascended into heaven, she longs to follow him; but remembering that her Bridegroom said, [[John 15:5|without me you can do nothing|Sine me nihil potestis facere]], she calls on his gracious help, saying: [[1:3|Draw me|Trahe me]] [[1:3|after thee|post te]]; that is, rouse and take away my sluggishness, kindle in me the ardour of thy charity, which ever draws upward, as fire rises on high; touch me with the savour of thy uncreated and boundless sweetness, so that I may be drawn purely and constantly to thee alone, cleave to thee always, and aspire to thee without ceasing; and so fulfil that exhortation of thy holy Apostle: [[Col 3:1|seek the things that are above, where Christ is sitting at the right hand of God|Quæ sursum sunt quærite, ubi Christus est in dextera Dei sedens]]; [[Col 3:2|Mind the things that are above, not the things that are upon the earth|quæ sursum sunt sapite, non quæ super terram]]. For I know, Lord Jesus, that thou hast said: [[John 12:32|if I be lifted up from the earth, will draw all things to myself|Si exaltatus fuero a terra, omnia traham ad me ipsum]]; and again: [[John 6:44|No man can come to me, except the Father, who hath sent me, draw him|Nemo potest venire ad me, nisi Pater, qui misit me, traxerit eum]]. Nor do I doubt that God thy Father and thou his Only-begotten are one drawer, as you are also one Creator. Again, I know that the Apostle truly said: We are not [[2 Cor 3:5|sufficient to think any thing of ourselves, as of ourselves: but our sufficiency is from God|sufficientes cogitare aliquid ex nobis, quasi ex nobis: sed sufficientia nostra ex Deo est]].

paras.t: Ecce, o sponse cœlestis, dulcissime Jesu, conatur spiritus meus tibi fideliter adhærere, in te conquiescere, tibi per contemplationem amorosam et contemplativum amorem sincere vacare; sed retrahunt, retardant, impediunt mille impedimenta. Intellectus enim instabilis est, ratio debilis, voluntas ad vana ac mala proclivis, sensualitas trahit deorsum, quotidianæ necessitates in terrenis me occupant sensibilibusque involvunt, exteriorum sensuum objecta alliciunt, acies vitiorum, mundus, et dæmonum turbæ, undique nos impugnant : et certe ambulo in medio laqueorum, in agmine gravissimorum periculorum, sed et moles miseræ carnis me deprimit. Quid igitur mihi incumbit? nisi ad tuam confugere gratiosissimam opem, et ex intimo cordis affectu orare : Trahe me post te, incessabiliter tange, perfunde, illustra, adjuva et conforta cor meum. Tu enim per Osee prophetam dixisti : In funiculis Adam traham eos, in vinculis caritatis ; item per Jeremiam : In caritate perpetua dilexi te ; ideo attraxi te miserans. Prævaleat in me, Domine, tractus iste; absit semper longe a me omnis tractus adulterium affectionis, et omnis irrationabilium passionum, suspicionum ac vitiorum impulsus.
paras.en: Behold, O heavenly Bridegroom, sweetest Jesus, my spirit strives to cleave faithfully to thee, to rest in thee, to give itself sincerely to thee through loving contemplation and contemplative love; but a thousand hindrances draw it back, slow it, and hinder it. For the understanding is unsteady, the reason weak, the will prone to vain and evil things; sensuality drags downward; daily needs busy me with earthly things and entangle me in things of sense; the objects of the outward senses allure; the battle line of the vices, the world and the hosts of demons assail us on every side. And truly I walk in the midst of snares, in a throng of the gravest dangers, and the weight of this wretched flesh too bears me down. What then is left to me, but to flee to thy most gracious help, and to pray from the inmost affection of the heart: [[1:3|Draw me|Trahe me]] [[1:3|after thee|post te]]; touch, steep, enlighten, help and strengthen my heart without ceasing. For thou hast said by the prophet Osee: [[Osee 11:4|I will draw them with the cords of Adam, with the bands of love|In funiculis Adam traham eos, in vinculis caritatis]]; and likewise by Jeremias: [[Jer 31:3|I have loved thee with an everlasting love, therefore have I drawn thee, taking pity on thee|In caritate perpetua dilexi te ; ideo attraxi te miserans]]. Let this drawing prevail in me, O Lord; and far from me be always every drawing of adulterous affection, and every impulse of irrational passions, suspicions and vices.

paras.t: Curremus in odore unguentorum tuorum : id est, si ita attraxeris me, ego et filiæ meæ ac animæ recenter conversæ, quibus gratiam mihi communicatam impertiri studebo, celeriter appropinquabimus tibi, et viam mandatorum tuorum curremus, igne amoris succensæ. Æstuanter quippe amanti nihil difficile, et ei qui gustavit quam multa sit abundantia dulcedinis tuæ, nihil molestius quam retardari a te, et a caritatis cursibus impediri. Curremus (inquam) in odore unguentorum tuorum, id est, affecti gustu interno supernorum charismatum, gratia et effectibus ecclesiasticorum sacramentorum, prægustatione cœlestium gaudiorum, affluentiaque donorum Spiritus Sancti. Hæc sunt unguenta valde suavia et præclara : ad quæ ut pertingere valeamus, oportet nos sequi vestigia in primis sanctæ humilitatis, patientiæ, mansuetudinis, passionisque Christi; et per veram contritionem cum beatissima Magdalene prosterni ad pedes sponsi cœlestis, eosque pœnitentiæ lacrimis ubertim lavare ac osculari; et inde per satisfactionem condignam, per spiritualem profectum, et jugem cordis custodiam, ad oscula manuum ejus consurgere : sicque ordinate per puræ ac fervidæ caritatis affectiones flammigeras, per incommutabilis Veritatis contemplationes sinceras, ad osculum oris ejus mundissimi cum summa veneratione accedere ; nec cum impiissimo traditore, polluta mente ad summæ Sanctitatis os deosculandum nos ipsos ingerere.
paras.en: [[1:3|We will run|Curremus]] [[1:3|to the odour of thy ointments|in odore unguentorum tuorum]]: that is, if thou draw me so, I and my daughters, the newly converted souls to whom I shall strive to impart the grace given to me, will swiftly draw near to thee, and, set on fire with love, we shall run [[Ps 118:32|the way of thy commandments|viam mandatorum tuorum]]. For to one who loves ardently nothing is hard; and to one who has tasted how great is the abundance of thy sweetness[[Ps 30:20||]], nothing is more grievous than to be held back from thee and hindered in the courses of charity. [[1:3|We will run|Curremus]] (I say) [[1:3|to the odour of thy ointments|in odore unguentorum tuorum]]: that is, moved by the inward taste of the heavenly gifts, by the grace and effects of the sacraments of the Church, by the foretaste of the joys of heaven, and by the abundance of the gifts of the Holy Ghost. These are ointments most sweet and excellent; and that we may be able to reach them, we must follow first of all in the footsteps of the holy humility, patience, meekness and passion of Christ; and through true contrition fall down with the most blessed Magdalen at the feet of the heavenly Bridegroom, and wash them abundantly with tears of penance and kiss them[[Luke 7:38||]]; and then, through worthy satisfaction, spiritual progress and constant guard of the heart, rise to the kisses of his hands; and so, in due order, through the flaming affections of pure and fervent charity and through sincere contemplations of the unchangeable Truth, draw near with the greatest reverence to the kiss of his most pure mouth: and not, like the most wicked traitor[[Matt 26:49||]], thrust ourselves forward with a defiled mind to kiss the mouth of the supreme Holiness.

paras.t: Quidam præinducta exponit de Synagoga, quantum ad exitum ejus de terra Ægypti. Quod non videtur congruere : quoniam Sancti veteris Testamenti, nec principaliter nec finaliter optaverunt liberationem illam ab Ægyptiaca servitute ; sed redemptionem a jugo peccati, a servitute diaboli, a reatu culpæ originalis, a spoliatione gloriæ æternalis : cujus redemptionis figura fuit liberatio ex Ægypto.
paras.en: A certain writer expounds the foregoing of the Synagogue, as to its going out of the land of Egypt. This does not seem to fit: for the Saints of the Old Testament did not desire, either chiefly or as their end, that deliverance from bondage in Egypt, but redemption from the yoke of sin, from the bondage of the devil, from the guilt of original sin, and from the loss of eternal glory; of which redemption the deliverance from Egypt was a figure.

paras.t: Sequitur vox Ecclesiæ ad adolescentulas. Introduxit me rex in cellaria sua : id est, per lucem et gratiam contemplationis erexit me ad incerta et occulta sapientiæ suæ intelligenda, in mysticos intellectus, ad theorias sublimes, ad intuenda abdita Scripturarum, ad speculandum consilium superbeatissimæ Trinitatis de modo salvationis generis humani, per incarnationem et passionem Verbi æterni. Deditque mihi fidem formatam cum rationibus credendorum et purificatæ mentis intelligentia, ut queam ea quæ fidei sunt, evangelizare, persuadere, declarare, defendere. Sicque introduxit me in sanctuarium suum, in amplitudinem divinarum illuminationum ; et per eminentem gradum doni sapientiæ, fecit me quasi secretariam et consiliariam suam rex meus et Deus meus. Insuper, Introduxit me in cellaria sua, ad contemplandas mansiones cœlestes ac gaudia civium supernorum, ut sciam non solum per fidem, sed etiam per prælibationem suavem, per experientiam certam, per revelationem supernaturalem, quæ sit spes vocationis nostræ, ita ut voce filiorum meorum pronuntiem : Nos autem revelata facie gloriam Domini contemplantes, in eamdem imaginem transformamur a claritate in claritatem. Nonne in ista cellaria fuit perductus Paulus usque in tertium cœlum raptus, ubi audivit verba arcana, quæ non licet homini loqui?
paras.en: There follows the voice of the Church to the young maidens. [[1:3|The king hath brought me into his storerooms|Introduxit me rex in cellaria sua]]: that is, by the light and grace of contemplation he has raised me up to understand [[Ps 50:8|the uncertain and hidden things|incerta et occulta]] of his wisdom [the margin gives Ps. i, 8; the words are from Ps 50:8], to mystical understandings, to sublime contemplations [Latin *theorias*, the Greek word for contemplation], to look into the hidden things of the Scriptures, to behold the counsel of the most blessed Trinity on the manner of the salvation of mankind through the incarnation and passion of the eternal Word. And he has given me formed faith [that is, faith given its life and form by charity], with the reasons for what is to be believed and the understanding of a purified mind, so that I can preach, commend, explain and defend the things of faith. And so my King and my God has brought me into his sanctuary, into the breadth of divine illuminations; and through the eminent degree of the gift of wisdom has made me, as it were, his secretary and counsellor. Moreover, he [[1:3|hath brought me into his storerooms|Introduxit me in cellaria sua]] to contemplate the heavenly mansions and the joys of the citizens above, so that I may know, not by faith alone but also by a sweet foretaste, by sure experience and by supernatural revelation, [[Eph 1:18|what the hope is|quæ sit spes]] of our calling; so that with the voice of my sons I may declare: But we, [[2 Cor 3:18|beholding the glory of the Lord with open face, are transformed into the same image from glory to glory|revelata facie gloriam Domini contemplantes, in eamdem imaginem transformamur a claritate in claritatem]]. Was it not into these storerooms that Paul was brought, [[2 Cor 12:2|caught up to the third heaven|usque in tertium cœlum raptus]], where he [[2 Cor 12:4|heard secret words which it is not granted to man to utter|audivit verba arcana, quæ non licet homini loqui?]]?

paras.t: Exsultabimus et lætabimur in te : id est, in contemplatione divitiarum gloriæ tuæ immensæ, et in amore bonitatis tuæ penitus infinitæ, tam vehementer lætabitur cor nostrum, non solum in patria, sed item in via, quod jucunditas ista redundabit in corpus : juxta illud Psalmi, Cor meum et caro mea exsultaverunt in Deum vivum. In spe quoque et prælibatione ac arrha felicitatis futuræ jam gloriamur, dicente Apostolo : Gloriamur in spe gloriæ filiorum Dei; et rursus : Scimus quoniam si terrena domus nostra habitationis hujus dissolvatur, quod ædificationem habemus ex Deo, domum non manufactam, æternam in cœlis. Etenim si in infimis istis sensibilibus rebus videtur alicui gloriandum, nonne incomparabiliter potius videtur gloriandum in superditissimo et superpulcherrimo fonte totius boni? in quo est omnium bonorum desiderabilium et pulcherrimorum plena et infinita possessio, in quo solo tota nostra salus consistit, de quo prædulci et decoro versiculo cantat Propheta : In Deo salutare meum, et gloria mea; Deus auxilii mei, et spes mea in Deo est. Lætabimur ergo in te, o sponse inclyte et decore, memores uberum tuorum, id est beneficiorum gratiæ tuæ, documentorum et præceptorum ac consiliorum tuorum, de quibus jam plenius dictum est, quibus nos alis, super vinum.
paras.en: [[1:3|we will be glad and rejoice in thee|Exsultabimus et lætabimur in te]]: that is, in the contemplation of the riches of thy boundless glory and in the love of thy wholly infinite goodness our heart will rejoice so vehemently, not only in our homeland but also on the way, that this gladness will overflow into the body; according to that word of the Psalm: [[Ps 83:3|My heart and my flesh have rejoiced in the living God|Cor meum et caro mea exsultaverunt in Deum vivum]]. In the hope too, and the foretaste and pledge of the happiness to come, we glory already, as the Apostle says: We [[Rom 5:2|glory in the hope of the glory of the sons of God|Gloriamur in spe gloriæ filiorum Dei]]; and again: [[2 Cor 5:1|we know, if our earthly house of this habitation be dissolved, that we have a building of God, a house not made with hands, eternal in heaven|Scimus quoniam si terrena domus nostra habitationis hujus dissolvatur, quod ædificationem habemus ex Deo, domum non manufactam, æternam in cœlis]]. For if anyone thinks there is glorying to be had in these lowest things of sense, is there not incomparably more to glory in the more than richest and more than most beautiful fountain of all good, in which is the full and infinite possession of all good things desirable and most beautiful, in which alone all our salvation stands; of which the Prophet sings in a most sweet and comely verse: [[Ps 61:8|In God is my salvation and my glory: he is the God of my help, and my hope is in God.|In Deo salutare meum, et gloria mea; Deus auxilii mei, et spes mea in Deo est]] We [[1:3|rejoice in thee|lætabimur in te]], then, O glorious and comely Bridegroom, [[1:3|remembering thy breasts|memores uberum tuorum]], that is, the benefits of thy grace, thy teachings, precepts and counsels, of which enough has been said already, with which thou dost nourish us, [[1:3|more than wine|super vinum]].

paras.t: Recti diligunt te, non solum amore naturali et acquisito, sed potius amore gratuito, supernaturali, infuso. Quum enim sis ipsa bonitatis essentia, bonitas pura et infinita, in infinitum pulchrior, dulcior, convenientior, amabilior universis ac singulis, a quo quidquid bonum et amabile est, omnem suam bonitatem ac amabilitatem sortitum est; quicumque non diligit te, sicut tu ipse jussisti, toto corde, omnino curvus, perversus, ingratus, insipiensque esse convincitur. Recti itaque, id est justi, qui exhibent unicuique quod ei tenentur, te diligunt: quoniam exhibent tibi se ipsos, et amori tuo ac cultui mancipant jam se totos, ad quod non solum ex tua bonitate, sed et ex beneficiis tuis quæ susceperunt, tenentur; et quia tu prior amasti eos, et præparasti eis te ipsum in præmium.
paras.en: [[1:3|the rightous love thee|Recti diligunt te]], not only with natural and acquired love, but rather with a love freely given, supernatural and infused. For since thou art the very essence of goodness, pure and infinite goodness, infinitely more beautiful, sweeter, more fitting and more lovable than all things together and each one, from whom whatever is good and lovable has received all its goodness and lovableness, whoever does not love thee as thou thyself hast commanded, [[Matt 22:37|with thy whole heart|toto corde]], is proved to be altogether crooked, perverse, ungrateful and foolish. [[1:3|The rightous|Recti]], then, that is, the just, who render to each what they owe him, [[1:3|love thee|te diligunt]]: for they render themselves to thee, and now give themselves wholly over to thy love and worship, to which they are bound not only by thy goodness but also by the benefits they have received from thee; and because thou didst first love them[[1 John 4:10||]][[1 John 4:19||]], and hast prepared thyself for them as their reward[[John 14:3||]].

paras.t: Nigra sum, sed formosa, o filiæ Jerusalem. Ecclesia nigram se nominat : Primo, quoniam multi imperfecti, fragiles et infirmi ac peccatores in ea sunt : propter quod Christus comparat eam sagenæ missæ in mare, et ex omni genere piscium congreganti. Secundo, quia et ipsi electi ac boni, quotidie et frequenter in venialibus peccant, et eorum justitiæ quasi pannus menstruatæ censentur. Tertio, quia in vita hac variis tribulationibus, tentationibus, adversitatibus exercentur. Verumtamen ipsa se formosam fatetur, quoniam semper multi virtuosi et sancti in ea consistunt, et omnes qui ei vere incorporantur, caritate virtutibusque infusis ac donis Spiritus Sancti ornantur. Habet etiam sacramenta, quibus quotidie renovatur ac pulchrificatur. Itaque, Nigra sum, sed formosa, o filiæ Jerusalem, id est, animæ, seu adolescentulæ ac particulares Ecclesiæ, sicut tabernacula Cedar : qui fuit secundus filius Ismaelis, et habitavit ipse Cedar cum sobole sua atque familia in tabernaculis et in solitudine, seu deserto; sicque tabernacula ejus foris quandoque deformia, utpote ventis imbribusque exposita, intus erant divitiis et pecoribus plena; sicut pelles Salomonis : quibus ipse domum suam thalamumve ornavit, aut tabernaculum Dei seu vasa ejus operuit. Melius tamen per Salomonem intelligitur Christus: cujus pelles sunt speciosi vestitus ministrorum suorum, et ornamenta cultus divini, mores quoque et exteriores gestus, incessus et apparatus ipsius Christi, quibus se ejus sponsa conformat pro posse. His etenim tanquam optimis pellibus vestitur ac decoratur Ecclesia. Denique, per tabernacula Cedar possunt intelligi perfidi et gentiles, quibus infidelis Judæa similem reputavit Ecclesiam, contemnens eamdem.
paras.en: [[1:4|I am black but beautiful, O ye daughters of Jerusalem|Nigra sum, sed formosa, o filiæ Jerusalem]]. The Church calls herself black: first, because there are in her many who are imperfect, frail and weak, and sinners; for which reason Christ compares her to [[Matt 13:47|a net cast into the sea, and gathering together of all kinds of fishes|sagenæ missæ in mare, et ex omni genere piscium congreganti]]. Secondly, because even the elect and the good sin daily and often in venial sins, and their justices are reckoned [[Is 64:6|as the rag of a menstruous woman|quasi pannus menstruatæ]].
