Moreover there are many properties of the dove for which the Church is likened and compared to it; these I pass over now, since the discussion will turn to this more fully below.

paras.t: Quod vero nunc de columbino Ecclesiæ visu inductum est, quidam specialiter de prælatis, doctoribus, et prædicatoribus ejus exponunt: qui appellantur Ecclesiæ oculi, quia per ipsos illuminat filios suos, et prospicit eis, ac præcavet. Prospicit, inquam, de necessariis ad salutem adipiscendis, et præcavet de periculorum eventibus; et ipsos qui alios habent dirigere et docere, oportet in omni prætacta columbina simplicitate ac visus sapientiali acumine esse præcipuos.
paras.en: What has now been brought in about the dovelike sight of the Church, some expound specially of her prelates, doctors and preachers, who are called the eyes of the Church, because through them she enlightens her sons, and looks out for them, and takes precautions for them: looks out, I say, for the things necessary to be obtained for salvation, and takes precautions against dangers as they arise; and they who have to direct and teach others must be foremost in all the aforesaid dovelike simplicity and in wise keenness of sight.

paras.t: Insuper sponsa ex tantis suis præconiis, ab infallibili sponso sibi adscriptis, nequaquam superbiens, imo magis se ipsam humilians ac sponso vicem rependens, subjungit: Ecce tu pulcher es, dilecte mi, et decorus. Quasi dicat: Tibi magis laus ista debetur, tu pulcher in deitatis natura, imo pulcherrimus et superpulcherrimus ipse: cujus deitas est pulchritudo penitus infinita, fons universi decoris et gratiositatis ac ordinis, cujus comparatione omnis pulchritudo creata, est velut deformitas. Tibi quoque Unigenito Patris pulchritudo appropriatur, sicut ait Hilarius: Species est in imagine. Tu es universorum primum exemplar, tu veritas, sapientia, splendor, character, ars rationibus plena, atque imago Genitoris æterni perfecta. Tu etiam pulcher es in tua humanitate: quam præ omni creatura superbenedicta Trinitas decoravit, dans ei spiritum non ad mensuram, et totam ejus capacitatem adimplens charismatibus gratiæ, virtutum, donorum, fructuum, beatitudinum, imo et beatifica fruitione, ac gratiis gratis datis. Nec decuit te, o Verbum æternum, nisi tam pulcherrimam humanitatem assumere, quam eodem instante talem fecisti ac assumpsisti. Denique ab omni peccato originali ac actuali immunis es, atque in summa sanctitate vixisti in sæculo isto, ac Patrem tuum præ cunctis creaturis plenissime honorasti. Tu speciosus forma præ filiis hominum: et quamvis propter me factus es opprobrium hominum, non habens speciem neque decorem, similisque leproso; hoc tamen absque tuo sustinuisti demerito, nec internam tuam minuit formositatem, sed ad majorem tui corporis cessit glorificationem: et quo propter me fuisti deformior, eo in corde meo es pulchrior.
paras.en: Further, the Bride, in no way puffed up by such great praises ascribed to her by the infallible Bridegroom, but rather humbling herself and repaying the Bridegroom in turn, adds: [[1:15|Behold thou art fair, my beloved, and comely|Ecce tu pulcher es, dilecte mi, et decorus]]. As if she said: This praise is owed rather to thee; thou art fair in the nature of the Godhead, nay most fair and fair above all fairness: whose Godhead is beauty wholly infinite, the fount of all comeliness, graciousness and order, in comparison with which all created beauty is as deformity. To thee also, the Only-begotten of the Father, beauty is appropriated [that is, ascribed to one Person by a likeness, though it is common to all three], as Hilary says: *Beauty is in the Image*. Thou art the first exemplar of all things, thou the truth, the wisdom, the splendour, the figure, the art full of reasons, and the perfect image of the eternal Begetter. Thou art fair also in thy humanity, which the superblessed Trinity adorned above every creature, giving it the Spirit not by measure[[John 3:34||]], and filling its whole capacity with the charisms of grace, of the virtues, gifts, fruits and beatitudes, nay even with the beatific enjoyment, and with graces freely given. Nor was it fitting for thee, O eternal Word, to assume any but a humanity so very fair, which in the same instant thou didst make such and didst assume. Lastly thou art free from all sin, original and actual, and didst live in this world in the highest holiness, and didst honour thy Father most fully above all creatures. [[Ps 44:3|Thou art beautiful above the sons of men|speciosus forma præ filiis hominum]]: and although for my sake thou wast made [[Ps 21:7|the reproach of men|opprobrium hominum]], having no beauty nor comeliness[[Is 53:2||]], and like [[Is 53:4|a leper|leproso]], yet this thou didst bear without any demerit of thine, nor did it lessen thy inward loveliness, but it turned to the greater glorification of thy body: and the more deformed thou wast for my sake, the fairer thou art in my heart.

paras.t: Ideo, Lectulus noster floridus: quia conjunctio nostra, pura et sancta est, spiritualis, divina ac cœliformis; et lectulus noster est pax pectoris, conscientiæ puritas, quies mentis, contemplatio amorosa, dilectio intuitiva et amplexiva. In his libenter et benignissime mecum quiescis, dum ab omni exteriori tumultu me abstraho, ab omni sanctitatis tuæ offensa abstineo, et tibi soli intendo. In pace etenim locus tuus, qui super quietum quiescis, et deliciæ tuæ sunt esse cum talibus filiis hominum.
paras.en: Therefore, [[1:15|Our bed is flourishing|Lectulus noster floridus]]: because our union is pure and holy, spiritual, divine and heavenly; and our bed is peace of breast, purity of conscience, quiet of mind, loving contemplation, love that gazes and embraces. In these thou restest willingly and most kindly with me, while I withdraw myself from all outward tumult, abstain from every offence against thy holiness, and attend to thee alone. For thy place is in peace[[Ps 75:3||]], thou who restest upon the quiet[[Is 66:1||]][[Is 66:2||]] [Denis follows the old Latin reading of Is 66:2, "upon whom shall I rest but upon the humble and quiet", not the Vulgate's], and thy delights are to be with such [[Prov 8:31|children of men|filiis hominum]].

paras.t: Tigna domorum nostrarum cedrina. Domus istæ sponsi et sponsæ, sunt particulares Ecclesiæ et congregationes devotæ: quarum tigna, sunt personæ quæ præsident, et subditos caritative sustentant, confortant, stabiliunt, quemadmodum tigna domum. Quæ personæ instar cedrorum crescunt in perfectione virtutum, et eminent auctoritate prælationum; stantque in monte Libano, videlicet candidissimo Jesu Christo, monte altissimo, cui jugiter innituntur: abstinent quoque a putrefactione peccati, et virtutum ac documentorum suorum odore ac vigore infernales fugant serpentes: quemadmodum cedrus imputribilis est naturæ, crescens in Libano monte, atque serpentes suo fugans odore.
paras.en: [[1:16|The beams of our houses are of cedar|Tigna domorum nostrarum cedrina]]. These houses of the Bridegroom and the Bride are the particular Churches and devout congregations: whose beams are the persons who preside, and charitably support, strengthen and steady their subjects, as beams do a house. These persons grow like cedars in the perfection of the virtues, and stand high in the authority of their prelacies; and they stand on Mount Libanus, that is, on the most white Jesus Christ [Libanus is interpreted *whiteness*], the highest mountain, on whom they lean continually: they abstain also from the rottenness of sin, and by the odour and vigour of their virtues and teachings put to flight the serpents of hell: just as the cedar is of an incorruptible nature, grows on Mount Libanus, and puts serpents to flight by its odour.

paras.t: Laquearia nostra cypressina. Per laquearia, quæ domum intrinsecus implent et ornant, boni subditi obedientesque filii exprimuntur: quæ cypressina dicuntur, quoniam sicut cypressus est arbor velociter crescens, bassa seu humilis, imputribilisque consistens, cujus fructus seu folia cum oleo cocta, nobile unguentum efficiunt: sic boni subditi ac obedientes, ex superiorum suorum exemplis virtuosis ac saluberrimis documentis, cito ac multum proficiunt, vitiorum infectionem devitant; atque intra suæ vocationis humilitatem manentes, præstant proximis exempla salubria, tanquam vitalia medicamenta, ac bonæ famæ odorem, tanquam dulcissima et curativa unguenta.
paras.en: [[1:16|our rafters of cypress trees|Laquearia nostra cypressina]] [*laquearia*, panelled ceilings]. By the rafters, which fill and adorn a house within, good subjects and obedient sons are expressed: and they are called of cypress because, as the cypress is a tree that grows swiftly, low or humble, and remains incorruptible, whose fruit or leaves boiled with oil make a noble ointment, so good and obedient subjects, from the virtuous examples and most wholesome teachings of their superiors, make swift and great progress and shun the infection of vices; and, remaining within the lowliness of their calling, they offer their neighbours wholesome examples, as life-giving medicines, and the odour of good fame, as most sweet and healing ointments.

1.title: EXPOSITIO EJUSDEM CAPITULI PRIMI, DE SPONSA PARTICULARI.
1.title_en: Exposition of the same first chapter: of the particular bride

paras.t: De triplici sponsa Christi, dictum est in prologo hujus opusculi, videlicet universali, particulari, et singulari: ita quod unaquæque anima in caritate exsistens, est Christi sponsa particularis, per fidem et caritatem desponsata eidem, et ei per Baptismi gratiam consecrata: quam Dominus et Salvator brachiis caritatis adstringit, ac infusione virtutum fecundat. Hinc asserit Augustinus, quod omnis anima est Christi sponsa, vel diaboli adultera: si enim in caritate est Christi, censetur sponsa ipsius; si vero mortali subjacet culpæ, adultera reputatur diaboli. Itaque quæ in isto Salomonis volumine de universali exponuntur Ecclesia, generalique sponsa, de particulari quoque sponsa tropologice explanantur. Verumtamen, quoniam juxta præhabita, in his Canticis canticorum tractatur de amore perfecto, ideo non de quacumque anima existente in caritate et gratia, sed de anima heroica, divina, perfecta, ecstatice amorosa, hæc proprie exponuntur: quam expositionem præcipue prosequitur Vercellensis venerabilis abbas, in libris divini et magni Dionysii studiosissimus, qui et eosdem in stilum planum redegit.
paras.en: Of the threefold bride of Christ, namely the universal, the particular and the singular, it was said in the prologue of this little work: so that every soul that is in charity is a particular bride of Christ, espoused to him by faith and charity and consecrated to him by the grace of Baptism; and the Lord and Saviour holds her fast in the arms of charity and makes her fruitful by the infusion of the virtues. Hence Augustine asserts that every soul is either the bride of Christ or the adulteress of the devil: for if it is in charity, it is counted Christ's bride; but if it lies under mortal sin, it is reckoned the devil's adulteress. And so the things that are expounded in this book of Solomon of the universal Church, the general bride, are also explained tropologically [that is, in the moral sense, as applying to the individual soul] of the particular bride. Yet since, as was said before, these Canticles of Canticles treat of perfect love, they are properly expounded not of any soul whatever that is in charity and grace, but of the heroic soul, divine, perfect, ecstatically loving. This is the exposition followed above all by the venerable abbot of Vercelli [that is, Thomas Gallus, abbot of St Andrew's at Vercelli], most devoted to the books of the divine and great Dionysius, who also put them into a plain style.

paras.t: Igitur anima contemplativa purgata, sancto amore flammigera, in creaturis nequaquam concupitam reperiens quietem, ideoque ad verum et incommutabile bonum, ad superessentialem et superpulcherrimum sponsum totis suspirans præcordiis, ex plenitudine sincerissimæ suæ affectionis eructat verbum bonum amoriferum et suave: Osculetur me, inquiens, osculo oris sui, id est sponsus ille dulcissimus, qui solus sufficit mihi, qui creavit me propter se; nec possum nisi in eo quiescere, qui solus totum meum affectum quietare potest et contentare. Hic talis ac tantus, osculetur me osculo oris sui, id est, se ipsum gratiosissime applicet mihi, meque pauperculam suæ incomparabilis et infinitæ excellentiæ dignetur immediate conjungere: tangendo et illuminando apicem intellectus mei ad contemplandum majestatem et sapientiam, veritatem ac pulchritudinem ejus prorsus immensam; accendendo quoque verticem voluntatis seu affectivæ meæ superioris, ad diligendum purissime, stabiliter ac intentissime bonitatem ipsius illimitatam, ad gustandum fontanam ejus dulcedinem, omni fundo, termino, ac mensura carentem, ad quiescendum in ejus amplexu mundissimo, quatenus tota ferar, transformer, absorbeatque in ipsum, atque in suæ beatitudinis exuberantissimo et immenso oceano rapta demergar.
paras.en: So the contemplative soul, purified, aflame with holy love, finding in creatures nowhere the rest she longs for, and therefore sighing with all her heart for the true and unchangeable good, for the superessential and surpassingly beautiful bridegroom, out of the fullness of her most sincere affection [[Ps 44:2|hath uttered a good word|eructat verbum bonum]], love-bearing and sweet, saying: [[1:1|Let him kiss me|Osculetur me]], she says, [[1:1|with the kiss of his mouth|osculo oris sui]]: that is, that most sweet bridegroom, who alone suffices me, who created me for himself; nor can I rest except in him, who alone can quiet and content all my affection. Let this one, so great and such as he is, [[1:1|kiss me with the kiss of his mouth|osculetur me osculo oris sui]]: that is, let him most graciously apply himself to me, and deign to join me, poor little one, immediately to his incomparable and infinite excellence: by touching and enlightening the summit of my intellect to contemplate his majesty and wisdom, his truth and his wholly immeasurable beauty; and by kindling the height of my will, or of my higher affective power, to love his unlimited goodness most purely, steadfastly and intently, to taste his fountain-like sweetness, which has no bottom, bound or measure, and to rest in his most pure embrace, so that I may be wholly carried, transformed and absorbed into him, and, rapt away, be plunged into the overflowing and boundless ocean of his beatitude.

paras.t: Sed unde, o paupercula anima, pingui materiæ huic intrusa, gravi corporis moli immersa, quæ in ordine intellectualium substantiarum es sicut materia prima in ordine rerum: unde tibi vel præsumptio, vel audacia, aut certe fiducia petendi hoc osculum ab eo, quem polus, tellus, pontusque metuunt, quem supernorum altitudines spirituum perhorrescunt, sub quo curvantur qui portant orbem? Denique, si præsumptuosum videtur petere osculum, non dicam gloriosissimæ virginis Mariæ Christiferæ, sed gloriosæ virginis Catharinæ reginæ, aut Ursulæ sanctæ: quanto magis præsumptuosum apparet, petere osculum Sancti Sanctorum, omnipotentisque Regis, cujus respectu totus mundus est velut pulvis exiguus? Ad hæc quid respondes, o anima, in hoc exsilio, in regione hac dissimilitudinis, in valle lacrimarum hac constituta, ubi si dixeris quod peccatum non habeas, te ipsam seducis?
paras.en: But whence, O poor little soul, thrust into this gross matter, sunk in the heavy mass of the body, who art in the order of intellectual substances as prime matter is in the order of things [prime matter: in scholastic philosophy, matter of itself without any form, pure potency, the lowest grade of being]: whence hast thou the presumption, or the boldness, or at least the confidence, to ask this kiss of him whom sky, earth and sea fear, before whom the heights of the spirits above tremble, [[Job 9:13|under whom they stoop that bear up the world|sub quo curvantur qui portant orbem]]? In short, if it seems presumptuous to ask a kiss, I will not say of the most glorious Virgin Mary, the bearer of Christ, but of the glorious virgin and queen Catharine, or of St Ursula: how much more presumptuous does it appear to ask a kiss of the Holy of Holies, the almighty King, in respect of whom the whole world is [[Is 40:15|as a little dust|velut pulvis exiguus]]? What answerest thou to this, O soul, set in this exile, in this region of unlikeness [Augustine's phrase for the soul's estrangement from God], in this vale of tears, where, if thou sayest that thou hast no sin, thou deceivest thyself[[1 John 1:8||]]?

paras.t: Responsio animæ. — Quid me revocas ab intuitu sponsi mei? Cur ab ejus amplexu me impedis? Quare ab ejus colloquio me avertis? Cur in his quæ omnem rationem transcendunt, exigis rationem? Ignoras quod caritatis ardor non arctetur lege communi? Nescis quod sicut excellentia sponsi hujus immensa est, sic et dignatio ejus prorsus sit infinita? Numquid minor est caritas ejus aut pietas, quam majestas? Nonne ipse creavit me ad obtinendum beatificum illud osculum oris sui in patria Beatorum, hoc est, ad intuendum eum per speciem, ad perfruendum æternaliter bonitate ac dulcedine sua, ad satietatem plenissimam, ab omni fastidio perenniter alienam? Ipse qui caritatem suam mihi infudit, ipse eamdem in me accendit ac stimulat, atque ad postulandum osculum oris sui excitat et inflammat. Non est volentis, neque currentis. Caritas separationis impatiens, me coarctat; consideratio, imo et experientia dignationis miserationisque sponsi, hanc parit fiduciam; fides quoque et recolentia præteritorum beneficiorum ipsius, me animat. Nonne ipse est, qui quum dives esset divitiis infinitis, dives omnipotentia, non pecunia, et tam magnus quod magnitudinis ejus non est finis, propter me factus est pauper et parvus? et certe tam pauper, quod non habuit ubi caput suum reclinaret: atque tam parvus, quod intra unius mundissimæ humillimæque virgunculæ viscera se reclusit; et captus est rhinoceros ille, cui nullus valet resistere, caritate ac puritate unius puellæ: qui deinceps obtulit se in mortem, ut ei in æternum conjungat, et ab ipso deoscules. En venter meus quasi mustum absque spiraculo, quod lagunculas novas dirumpit, et coarctat me spiritus uteri mei. Loquar ergo ad sponsum, et respirabo paululum: et nunc agitante me desiderio erumpente, dicam semel, Osculetur me osculo oris sui; dicam secundo, Osculetur me osculo oris sui: addam et tertio, Osculetur me osculo oris sui.
paras.en: The soul's answer. — Why dost thou call me back from gazing on my bridegroom? Why dost thou hinder me from his embrace? Why dost thou turn me away from converse with him? Why dost thou demand a reason in things that pass all reason? Knowest thou not that the ardour of charity is not confined by the common law? Knowest thou not that as the excellence of this bridegroom is immeasurable, so his condescension is wholly infinite? Is his charity or his kindness less than his majesty? Did he not create me to obtain that beatific kiss of his mouth in the fatherland of the Blessed, that is, to behold him face to face [literally 'by sight', as opposed to by faith], to enjoy his goodness and sweetness for ever, to the fullest satiety, for ever free from all weariness? He who poured his charity into me, he it is that kindles and spurs it in me, and rouses and inflames me to ask for the kiss of his mouth. It is [[Rom 9:16|not of him that willeth, nor of him that runneth|Non est volentis, neque currentis]]. Charity, impatient of separation, presses me; the thought, nay, the experience, of the bridegroom's condescension and mercy begets this confidence; and faith, and the remembrance of his past benefits, give me heart. Is it not he who, [[2 Cor 8:9|being rich|quum dives esset]] with infinite riches, rich in omnipotence, not in money, and so great that [[Ps 144:3|of his greatness there is no end|magnitudinis ejus non est finis]] [the margin gives Ps. cxlv, 3; the words are Ps 144:3], for my sake [[2 Cor 8:9|he became poor|factus est pauper]] and little? So poor indeed that he [[Matt 8:20|hath not where to lay his head|non habuit ubi caput suum reclinaret]]; and so little that he shut himself up within the womb of one most pure and most humble little maiden; and that rhinoceros whom none can withstand was taken by the charity and purity of one girl [the bestiaries tell of the rhinoceros or unicorn, which no hunter can take, but which lays its head in the lap of a virgin and so is caught]: who then offered himself to death[[Is 53:12||]], that he might join me to himself for ever, and that I might be kissed by him. [[Job 32:19|Behold, my belly is as new wine which wanteth vent, which bursteth the new vessels|En venter meus quasi mustum absque spiraculo, quod lagunculas novas dirumpit]], and [[Job 32:18|the spirit of my bowels straiteneth me|coarctat me spiritus uteri mei]]. [[Job 32:20|I will speak|Loquar]], then, to the bridegroom, [[Job 32:20|and take breath a little|et respirabo paululum]]; and now, as desire bursting forth drives me on, I will say once, [[1:1|Let him kiss me with the kiss of his mouth|Osculetur me osculo oris sui]]; I will say a second time, [[1:1|Let him kiss me with the kiss of his mouth|Osculetur me osculo oris sui]]; and I will add a third time, [[1:1|Let him kiss me with the kiss of his mouth|Osculetur me osculo oris sui]].

paras.t: Responsio. — Numquid ebria es, quia sic loqueris? nec continens te saltem rubore? Nonne discretio mater est et auriga virtutum, sine qua etiam caritas ipsa præcipitat?
paras.en: Reply. — Art thou drunk, that thou speakest so, not restraining thyself even out of shame? Is not discretion the mother and charioteer of the virtues, without which even charity itself rushes headlong?

paras.t: Anima. — Ebria sum, inebriata refectione et potu illius a quo audies infra: Comedite, amici, et bibite; et inebriamini, carissimi. Denique ignara mihi videris juris ac proprietatum viriumque amoris. Non audisti Prophetam illum in utero matris sanctificatum, dicentem, Factus est sermo Domini in corde meo quasi ignis exæstuans, claususque in ossibus meis, et defeci, ferre non sustinens? Et rursus: Factus sum, inquit, quasi vir ebrius, et quasi homo madidus vino, a facie Domini et a facie verborum sanctorum ejus. Si sermo Domini sic inebriat et accendit, quanto magis amor ipsius? Præterea audi quid horum expertus dicat sanctus et dulcis ille Bernardus: O quanta vis amoris! o quanta in spiritu libertatis fiducia! Desiderio feror, ratione non ducor. Non putetur præsumptio, ubi viget ac dominatur affectio. Reclamat pudor: sed superat amor. Non ignoro quod honor regis judicium diligit; sed præceps amor nec judicium præstolatur, nec consilio temperatur, nec pudore frenatur, nec rationi subjicitur. Ideo tibi respondeo, quod in hac re discretio est, esse sine discretione: quoniam fons omnis discretionis paracletus Spiritus Sanctus, qui infundit, prævenit et inflammat, ipse utique custodit, dirigit et gubernat. Sed nunc argumentatio relinquatur, ne mens mea a sponso diutius impediatur. Etenim eo ipso quo dixi, Osculetur me osculo oris sui, ab eo me tangi, affici, oscularique sensi: ideo te relicta, loquar ad ipsum.
paras.en: The soul. — I am drunk, made drunk with the refreshment and the drink of him from whom thou shalt hear below: [[Cant 5:1|eat, O friends, and drink, and be inebriated, my dearly beloved|Comedite, amici, et bibite; et inebriamini, carissimi]]. In short, thou seemest to me ignorant of the law, the properties and the powers of love. Hast thou not heard that Prophet who was sanctified in his mother's womb, saying: The word of the Lord [[Jer 20:9|came in my heart as a burning fire, shut up in my bones, and I was wearied, not being able to bear it|in corde meo quasi ignis exæstuans, claususque in ossibus meis, et defeci, ferre non sustinens]]? And again: [[Jer 23:9|I am become|Factus sum]], he says, [[Jer 23:9|as a drunken man, and as a man full of wine, at the presence of the Lord, and at the presence of his holy words|quasi vir ebrius, et quasi homo madidus vino, a facie Domini et a facie verborum sanctorum ejus]]. If the word of the Lord so inebriates and inflames, how much more his love? Hear, moreover, what that holy and sweet Bernard, who had experience of these things, says: O how great is the power of love! O how great the confidence of the spirit of liberty! I am carried by desire, I am not led by reason. Let it not be thought presumption where affection thrives and rules. Shame protests, but love prevails. I know well that [[Ps 98:4|the king's honour loveth judgment|honor regis judicium diligit]]; but headlong love neither waits for judgment, nor is tempered by counsel, nor bridled by shame, nor made subject to reason. Therefore I answer thee that in this matter discretion is to be without discretion: for the fount of all discretion, the Paraclete, the Holy Ghost, who pours in, goes before and inflames, he himself also guards, directs and governs. But now let argument be left aside, lest my mind be kept any longer from the bridegroom. For in the very act of saying, [[1:1|Let him kiss me with the kiss of his mouth|Osculetur me osculo oris sui]], I felt myself touched, moved and kissed by him: therefore, leaving thee, I will speak to him.

paras.t: Quia meliora sunt ubera tua vino: id est, illuminatio tuæ veritatis æternæ, qua tu ipse intellectum immediate illuminas, ungis, ac doces: et inflammatio qua in me caritatem accendis: pietas qua tam benignissime refoves, consolaris, et confortas me, desiderabiliores ac dulciores sunt mihi vino, id est omni consolatione carnali, omnique instructione angelica et humana; fragrantia unguentis optimis, id est spiritualibus charismatibus eis adjunctis. Nempe ubera ista ad omnium carnalium voluptatum ducunt contemptum, ad tædium terrenorum, ad desiderium exercitationis internæ, ad ampliorem cordis custodiam, ad profundiorem sui ipsius humiliationem. Et hæc unguenta sunt optima, coram Deo et omnibus Sanctis suavissime redolentia, a peccatis præservativa, omniumque invisibilium curativa languorum. Hoc beatus Augustinus expertus, disseruit: Te, Domine Jesu Christe, cor meum introeunte, irradiante et oblectante, subito factum est mihi facile voluptatibus illis carere, quas ante metuebam relinquere.
paras.en: [[1:1|For thy breasts are better than wine|Quia meliora sunt ubera tua vino]]: that is, the enlightenment of thy eternal truth, by which thou thyself immediately enlightenest, anointest and teachest the intellect; and the burning by which thou kindlest charity in me; and the kindness with which thou so very graciously cherishest, consolest and strengthenest me: these are more desirable and sweeter to me than wine, that is, than all carnal consolation and all angelic and human instruction; [[1:2|smelling sweet of the best ointments|fragrantia unguentis optimis]], that is, of the spiritual gifts [charismata] joined to them. For these breasts lead to contempt of all carnal pleasures, to weariness of earthly things, to desire for inward exercise, to a closer guard of the heart, to a deeper humbling of oneself. And these ointments are the best, most sweetly fragrant before God and all the Saints, preserving from sins, and healing all invisible sicknesses. Blessed Augustine, having experienced this, said: When thou, Lord Jesus Christ, didst enter my heart, shining in it and delighting it, it suddenly became easy for me to go without those pleasures which before I feared to give up.

paras.t: Oleum effusum nomen tuum. Tu, o sponse, vocaris virtus et sapientia Dei Patris, tu appellaris Filius Virginis, tu Creator Salvatorque diceris; de te Isaias prædixit: Vocabitur nomen ejus, Admirabilis, Consiliarius, Deus, Fortis, Pater futuri sæculi, Princeps pacis: et quocumque nomine designeris, dulcescit clarescitque nomen hoc mihi, fulget in corde, ac pretiosissimum reputatur a me. Ideo adolescentulæ dilexerunt te, tua suavitate attractæ. Istæ adolescentulæ, sunt animæ proficientes, meritis quotidie abundantes: quæ increatæ dulcedinis gustum aliquantulum perceperunt, et ex eo ad meliora sunt provocatæ, et ad amandum magis accensæ, præsertim quoniam audierunt tot et tanta bona narrari de sponso. Frequenter enim contingit, quod multa laudabilia audiendo de aliquo nunquam viso, accendamur ipsius amore, et ædificemur in eo: quanto magis in amore sponsi cœlestis, ex fama ipsius debemus succendi? cujus præconia in Scripturis leguntur, cujus virtutes undique prædicantur; in quo scimus perfectionem simpliciter infinitam consistere, secundum deitatis suæ naturam qua æqualis est Patri, virtutes quoque creatas, in extremo excellentiæ termino, quo possunt creaturæ inesse, et hoc, secundum ipsius humanitatem.
paras.en: [[1:2|Thy name is as oil poured out|Oleum effusum nomen tuum]]. Thou, O bridegroom, art called [[1 Cor 1:24|the power of God and the wisdom of God|virtus et sapientia Dei]] the Father; thou art named the Son of the Virgin[[Luke 2:7||]]; thou art called Creator and Saviour[[Is 43:11||]] [the margin here reads '48. 11', perhaps for Is. xliii, 11, 'there is no saviour besides me']; of thee Isaias foretold: [[Is 9:6|his name shall be called Wonderful, Counsellor, God the Mighty, the Father of the world to come, the Prince of Peace|Vocabitur nomen ejus, Admirabilis, Consiliarius, Deus, Fortis, Pater futuri sæculi, Princeps pacis]]: and by whatever name thou art denoted, this name grows sweet and bright to me, shines in my heart, and is held by me most precious. [[1:2|therefore young maidens have loved thee|Ideo adolescentulæ dilexerunt te]], drawn by thy sweetness. These young maidens are the souls that are making progress, abounding daily in merits, who have had some little taste of the uncreated sweetness, and from it have been stirred on to better things and kindled to love more, especially since they have heard so many and such great goods told of the bridegroom. For it often happens that, hearing many praiseworthy things of someone we have never seen, we are kindled with love of him and edified in him: how much more ought we to be set on fire with love of the heavenly bridegroom from his fame? whose praises are read in the Scriptures, whose virtues are proclaimed on every side; in whom we know that there is perfection simply infinite, according to the nature of his Godhead, in which he is equal to the Father[[Phil 2:6||]], and also created virtues at the utmost limit of excellence at which they can be in a creature, and this according to his humanity.

paras.t: Trahe me post te: id est, da mihi lucem et gratiam contemplationis tam altæ, ac tantum sanctæ caritatis ardorem, ut cuncta creata transcendam, et tibi soli inhæream; sicque abstractus et absolutus ab omnibus, tam vehementer tibi intentus sim, ut ceterorum omnium obliviscar, imo neque me ipsum, nec proprias actiones advertam. Nam ut sanctus pater ait Antonius, Perfecte non orat, qui in oratione sua non ita in Deum extenditur, nec tam valenter in eum defigitur, ut immemor omnium reliquorum reddatur.
paras.en: [[1:3|Draw me|Trahe me]] [[1:3|after thee|post te]] [Denis joins 'after thee' to 'Draw me'; the Douay-Rheims reads 'Draw me: we will run after thee']: that is, give me the light and grace of contemplation so high, and so great an ardour of holy charity, that I may pass beyond all created things and cleave to thee alone; and so, drawn away and set free from all things, I may be so intently fixed on thee that I forget all else, nay, that I take no notice even of myself or of my own acts. For as the holy father Antony says: He does not pray perfectly who in his prayer is not so stretched out towards God, nor so strongly fixed on him, that he is made forgetful of all else.

paras.t: Curremus in odore unguentorum tuorum. De unguentis jam dictum est super illud, Fragrantia unguentis optimis. Præterea omnium actiones virtutum, unguenta sunt, evangelicorum quoque impletiones consiliorum: ideo unguenta optima rite censentur actus excellentissimarum virtutum, utpote fidei, spei et caritatis. Item optima unguenta, sunt actus virtutum, secundum gradum earum supremum: sic unguenta bona, sunt actus boni ac meritorii incipientium; unguenta meliora, actus laudabiles proficientium; unguenta optima, perfectorum. Postremo unguenta bona, sunt opera virtutum moralium; unguenta meliora, virtutum intellectualium; optima, theologicarum. Porro odores unguentorum istorum, sunt delectationes puræ actibus virtuosis annexæ: in quibus odoribus currimus, quando præ gaudio spirituali et consolatione cœlesti, quas in Dei cultu ac honorificentia experimur, Deo cum ingenti promptitudine ac celeritate obsequimur, juxta illud Josue, Servite ei corde perfecto atque verissimo. Qui sic currit ad beatitudinis suæ indeficientissimum fontem, mox ut de bassitudine carnis mortalis exierit, ad cœlestis palatii perveniet montem. Ad quod exhortans Apostolus: Sic, inquit, currite ut comprehendatis. Qui sic velox est in opere suo, coram Rege cœlorum stabit; et sequetur ejus vestigia, qui exsultavit ut gigas ad currendam viam. Talem cursum non redarguit sanctus Job, quamvis Eliu hoc ei imposuerit, dicens: Dixit enim, Non placebit homo Deo, etiam si cucurrerit cum eo. Cum ita currente, currit et sponsus: qui cum pergentibus pergit, cum currentibus currit, cum volantibus volat, suas nullibi relinquens dilectas. Ad quem cursum inter prospera et adversa infatigabiliter peragendum, hortatur nos Paulus, loquens: Curramus propositum nobis iter, adspicientes in auctorem fidei et consummatorem Jesum, qui proposito sibi gaudio, sustinuit crucem, confusione contempta. Recogitate eum, qui talem sustinuit a peccatoribus adversus semetipsum contradictionem, ut non fatigemini animis vestris deficientes.
paras.en: [[1:3|We will run|Curremus]] [[1:3|to the odour of thy ointments|in odore unguentorum tuorum]]. Of the ointments something has been said already, on the words [[1:2|Smelling sweet of the best ointments|Fragrantia unguentis optimis]]. Further, the acts of all the virtues are ointments, and so are the fulfilments of the evangelical counsels: hence the best ointments are rightly taken to be the acts of the most excellent virtues, namely faith, hope and charity. Again, the best ointments are the acts of the virtues in their highest degree: so the good ointments are the good and meritorious acts of beginners; the better ointments, the praiseworthy acts of those making progress; the best ointments, those of the perfect. Lastly, the good ointments are the works of the moral virtues; the better, of the intellectual virtues; the best, of the theological. Now the odours of these ointments are the pure delights joined to virtuous acts: and we run in these odours when, for the spiritual joy and heavenly consolation that we experience in the worship and honour of God, we serve God with great readiness and speed, according to the word of Josue: [[Jos 24:14|serve him with a perfect and most sincere heart|Servite ei corde perfecto atque verissimo]]. He who runs thus to the most unfailing fountain of his beatitude will, as soon as he has gone out of the lowliness of mortal flesh, come to the mountain of the heavenly palace. Exhorting us to this, the Apostle says: [[1 Cor 9:24|So|Sic]], he says, [[1 Cor 9:24|run that you may obtain|currite ut comprehendatis]]. He who is thus [[Prov 22:29|swift in his work|velox est in opere suo]] shall stand before the King of heaven, and shall follow the footsteps of him who [[Ps 18:6|rejoiced as a giant to run the way|exsultavit ut gigas ad currendam viam]]. Such running holy Job did not condemn, although Eliu laid this to his charge, saying: [[Job 34:9|For he hath said: Man shall not please God, although he run with him|Dixit enim, Non placebit homo Deo, etiam si cucurrerit cum eo]]. With one who runs thus the bridegroom runs too: who goes with those who go, runs with those who run, flies with those who fly, nowhere leaving his beloved ones. To this race, to be run untiringly amid prosperity and adversity, Paul exhorts us, saying: Let us run the course set before us[[Heb 12:1||]], [[Heb 12:2|Looking on Jesus, the author and finisher of faith, who, having joy set before him, endured the cross, despising the shame|adspicientes in auctorem fidei et consummatorem Jesum, qui proposito sibi gaudio, sustinuit crucem, confusione contempta]]. [[Heb 12:3|think diligently upon him that endured such opposition from sinners against himself that you be not wearied, fainting in your minds|Recogitate eum, qui talem sustinuit a peccatoribus adversus semetipsum contradictionem, ut non fatigemini animis vestris deficientes]].

paras.t: Sic Deus immensus, sua naturali infinitaque bonitate ac amabilitate trahit ad se et in se suos electos, quemadmodum libro de Divinis nominibus Dionysius protestatur: Deus sua supersubstantiali bonitate et appetibilitate (per quam est omnium attractivus) suum ingignit amorem menti creatæ.
paras.en: Thus the immeasurable God, by his natural and infinite goodness and lovableness, draws his elect to himself and into himself, as Dionysius declares in the book On the Divine Names: God, by his supersubstantial goodness and desirability (by which he draws all things to himself), begets his love in the created mind.

paras.t: Denique sponsa in his exaudita, grato corde subjungit: Introduxit me rex in cellaria sua, id est, divitias gloriæ suæ mihi ostendit, infinitam opulentiam suam monstravit, affluentiam gratiæ mihi in præsenti paratæ, et supereffluentiam gloriæ mihi in futuro præstandæ, si ei perseveravero, revelavit. Unde et S. Agnes asseruit: Ostendit mihi thesauros incomparabiles. Hoc fit, dum mens introducitur in sanctuarium Dei, id est, luce contemplationis perfunditur, ad intuendum quam infinite deliciosus, perfectus et felix sit Deus altissimus in se ipso, quam inæstimabilis sit liberalitas ejus ad dandum, quam supercopiosa ad remunerandum: ex qua consideratione oritur gaudium grande.
paras.en: Then the bride, heard in these things, adds with a grateful heart: [[1:3|The king hath brought me into his storerooms|Introduxit me rex in cellaria sua]]: that is, he has shown me the riches of his glory, displayed his infinite wealth, and revealed the abundance of grace prepared for me in the present and the superabundance of glory to be bestowed on me in the future, if I persevere with him. Hence St Agnes too declared: He hath shown me incomparable treasures. This happens when the mind is brought into the sanctuary of God, that is, is flooded with the light of contemplation, to behold how infinitely delightful, perfect and happy the most high God is in himself, how inestimable his liberality in giving, how superabundant in rewarding: and from this consideration great joy arises.

paras.t: Unde subjungitur: Exsultabimus et lætabimur in te: non in nobis, sed in te universorum bonorum datore. Gloriabimur, tuæ infinitæ felicitati congratulando: et quo quis magis te diligit, eo utique omni perfectioni et excellentiæ tuæ cordialius frequentiusque congaudet. Et hæc est gloriatio optima, ex puro Deitatis amore procedens. Exsultabimus quoque, quia tu, rex cœlorum, creator universorum, prior dilexisti nos; et quia tu, noster creator ac judex, factus es noster salvator et advocatus: et quia tu, munificentissime sponse, tot et tanta nobis beneficia contulisti, majoraque promisisti, quorum nequaquam oblivisci debemus.
paras.en: Hence it is added: [[1:3|we will be glad and rejoice in thee|Exsultabimus et lætabimur in te]]: not in ourselves, but in thee, the giver of all goods. We will glory, rejoicing with thee in thy infinite happiness; and the more one loves thee, the more heartily and the more often he rejoices with thee in all thy perfection and excellence. And this is the best glorying, proceeding from pure love of the Godhead. [[1:3|We will be glad|Exsultabimus]] also because thou, the King of heaven, the creator of all things, hast first loved us[[1 John 4:10||]][[1 John 4:19||]] [the margin gives Joann. iv, 10, 19, that is, the First Epistle of John]; and because thou, our creator and judge, hast become our saviour and advocate; and because thou, most bountiful bridegroom, hast bestowed on us so many and such great benefits, and promised greater, which we must by no means forget.

paras.t: Propter quod subditur: Memores uberum tuorum, id est, nos memores exsistentes caritatis pietatisque tuæ et miserationum ac consolationum, illuminationum ac visitationum tuarum, quibus nos jugiter reficis, exsultabimus et lætabimur in te: juxta illud Psalmi, Memor fui Dei, et delectatus sum. Gratitudo hæc semper meretur majora, juxta quod sponsus fatetur: Habenti dabitur, et abundabit.
paras.en: For this reason it is added: [[1:3|remembering thy breasts|Memores uberum tuorum]]: that is, being mindful of thy charity and kindness, and of thy mercies and consolations, thy enlightenments and visitations, with which thou dost ever refresh us, [[1:3|we will be glad and rejoice in thee|exsultabimus et lætabimur in te]]; according to the word of the Psalm: [[Ps 76:4|I remembered God, and was delighted|Memor fui Dei, et delectatus sum]]. This gratitude always merits greater things, as the bridegroom declares: To [[Matt 25:29|every one that hath shall be given, and he shall abound|Habenti dabitur, et abundabit]].

paras.t: Insuper, quoniam memoria beneficiorum accendit amorem, secundum illud Psalmi, In meditatione mea exardescet ignis, recte subjungit: Recti diligunt te. Tu enim es primum et summum amabile, causa et ratio omnis amabilitatis ac boni amoris: idcirco obliquus et curvus est, qui te non amat. Nec sufficit amor tuus quicumque, sed necessarius est amor spiritualis, meritorius, et infusus, quem soli recti, id est justi, habent ad te. Justi quippe sunt, qui tua observant præcepta: et hi soli vere te diligunt, sicut tu ipse testaris: Si quis diligit me, sermonem meum servabit; itemque, Qui habet mandata mea et servat ea, ille est qui me diligit. Hæc rectitudo meretur exaudiri a Domino, juxta illud Job: Si mundus et rectus incesseris, statim evigilabit ad te.
paras.en: Moreover, since the remembrance of benefits kindles love, according to the word of the Psalm, [[Ps 38:4|in my meditation a fire shall flame out|In meditatione mea exardescet ignis]], she rightly adds: [[1:3|the rightous love thee|Recti diligunt te]] [recti, 'the right' or 'upright', which the next sentences play on with 'crooked' and 'rectitude']. For thou art the first and highest lovable thing, the cause and ground of all lovableness and of all good love: therefore he who does not love thee is twisted and crooked. Nor does just any love of thee suffice; what is needed is a love that is spiritual, meritorious and infused, which only the upright, that is, the just, have towards thee. For the just are those who keep thy commandments; and these alone truly love thee, as thou thyself testifiest: [[John 14:23|If any one love me, he will keep my word|Si quis diligit me, sermonem meum servabit]]; and again: [[John 14:21|He that hath my commandments and keepeth them; he it is that loveth me|Qui habet mandata mea et servat ea, ille est qui me diligit]]. This uprightness merits to be heard by the Lord, according to the word of Job: [[Job 8:6|If thou wilt walk clean and upright, he will presently awake unto thee|Si mundus et rectus incesseris, statim evigilabit ad te]].

paras.t: Nigra sum, sed formosa, filiæ Jerusalem. Quanto anima fervida sanctitatem et pulchritudinem Dei ac sponsi sui limpidius contemplatur, tanto propriam parvitatem, imperfectionem, insufficientiamque clarius intuetur, humiliusque fatetur. Idcirco a contemplatione sanctissimi et superpulcherrimi sponsi sui rediens ac suspensa, nigram se clamat, sciens quod cœli non sint mundi, nec stellæ splendeant respectu illius. Insuper, juxta divini Dionysii documenta in pluribus locis, perfectissima unio atque cognitio, qua mens Deo conjungitur in hac vita, est per omnem abnegationem ab ipso, ac per omnimodam ignorantiam ejus, quantum ad quid est, ita quod ei unitur tanquam prorsus ignoto. Propter quod dicitur in caligine esse: ob quam dicit se nigram, quia caligo videtur esse quædam nigredo. Nihilo minus asserit se formosam, quia hæc ipsa tam humilis propriæ defectuositatis confessio, supplet ejus defectum, et ipsam perornat. Et quamvis respectu sponsi sit nigra, tamen in suo genere est formosa: quoniam sponsus non requirit ab ea puritatem et perfectionem virtutum, nisi secundum exigentiam facultatis, professionis, vocationis, seu status ipsius sponsæ: ideo admonet eam, ut secundum suam vocationem ambulet digne Deo. Sed quomodo anima peccans quotidie asserit se formosam? Respondetur, quod formosa est secundum modum viæ, non patriæ; et per exclusionem omnis mortalis, non venialis, peccati; et quia de suis venialibus assidue pœnitet ac purgatur, ita quod quotidie amplius proficit, quam decrescat. Et juxta hunc sensum sanctus Job fatebatur: Neque reprehendit me cor meum in omni vita mea.
paras.en: [[1:4|I am black but beautiful, O ye daughters of Jerusalem|Nigra sum, sed formosa, filiæ Jerusalem]]. The more clearly the fervent soul contemplates the holiness and beauty of God, her bridegroom, the more clearly she beholds her own littleness, imperfection and insufficiency, and the more humbly she confesses it. Therefore, returning from the contemplation of her most holy and more than most beautiful bridegroom, and held in suspense, she cries out that she is black, knowing that [[Job 15:15|the heavens are not pure|cœli non sint mundi]], nor do the stars shine, in comparison with him[[Job 25:4||]][[Job 25:5||]]. Moreover, according to the teaching of the divine Dionysius in many places, the most perfect union and knowledge by which the mind is joined to God in this life is by way of every negation from him, and by an utter unknowing of him as to what he is, so that it is united to him as to one wholly unknown. For this reason it is said to be in darkness [*caligo*, the cloud or darkness of the mystical theology]: and because of this she says that she is black, since darkness seems to be a kind of blackness. None the less she declares that she is beautiful, for this very confession, so humble, of her own defectiveness makes up for her defect and adorns her. And though she is black in comparison with the bridegroom, yet in her own kind she is beautiful: for the bridegroom does not require of her purity and perfection of the virtues except as the capacity, profession, vocation or state of the bride herself demands; and so he admonishes her that, according to her vocation, she [[Col 1:10|walk worthy of God|ambulet digne Deo]]. But how does a soul that sins daily declare herself beautiful? The answer is that she is beautiful after the manner of the way, not of the fatherland [that is, of this pilgrim life, not of the glory of heaven]; and by the exclusion of every mortal sin, though not of venial sin; and because she continually repents of her venial sins and is cleansed of them, so that each day she makes more progress than she falls back. And in this sense holy Job confessed: [[Job 27:6|my heart doth not reprehend me in all my life|Neque reprehendit me cor meum in omni vita mea]].

paras.t: Quoniam itaque comparatione sponsi, anima sancta affirmat se nigram, adjecit: Quia decoloravit me sol, id est, comparatione ipsius deformem me sentio, qui solus incircumscriptibiliter lucet, et incomparabiliter sanctus est.
paras.en: Since, then, the holy soul affirms that she is black in comparison with the bridegroom, she adds: [[1:5|because the sun hath altered my colour|Quia decoloravit me sol]], that is, I feel myself unsightly in comparison with him who alone shines without limit and is holy beyond compare.

paras.t: Præterea anima contemplativa Christi sponsa, ex parte supremæ suæ portionis intellectivæque partis, ait: Filii matris meæ, id est potentiæ et affectiones et actus sensitivæ partis, appetitusque concupiscibilis et irascibilis, et passiones earum, sensus quoque exteriores et interiores, pugnaverunt contra me. Caro enim concupiscit adversus spiritum, et carnalia desideria militant contra animam, id est contra partem ejus superiorem. Similiter sensus exteriores repræsentationibus objectorum suorum et incustodia sua mentem non parum impugnant: ita quod mors ingreditur per fenestras, et oculus animam deprædatur. Porro sensitiva pars, mater intellectivæ partis vocatur, quia cognitio nostra intellectiva exordium sumit a sensitiva; et omnium potentiarum, affectionum et actionum suarum ipsa anima dicitur mater, quia fluunt ab ea, et ipsa illarum subjectum est et origo. Sensus etiam interiores suis imaginationibus atque tumultibus varia pariunt impedimenta recollectionis devotionisque menti. Propter quod anima per superiores suas vires se custodire, inferioresque vires regere necessario indiget.
paras.en: Further, the contemplative soul, the bride of Christ, speaking from her highest portion, the intellective part, says: [[1:5|the sons of my mother|Filii matris meæ]], that is, the powers, affections and acts of the sensitive part, the concupiscible and irascible appetites [that is, the appetite that seeks what is pleasant and the appetite that meets what is hard] and their passions, and the outer and inner senses too, [[1:5|have fought against me|pugnaverunt contra me]]. For [[Gal 5:17|the flesh lusteth against the spirit|Caro enim concupiscit adversus spiritum]], and [[1 Pet 2:11|carnal desires which war against the soul|carnalia desideria militant contra animam]], that is, against its higher part. Likewise the outer senses, by the images of their objects and by being left unguarded, assail the mind not a little: so that [[Jer 9:21|death is come up through our windows|mors ingreditur per fenestras]], and [[Lam 3:51|my eye hath wasted my soul|oculus animam deprædatur]] [Denis: "death enters by the windows, and the eye plunders the soul"]. Now the sensitive part is called the mother of the intellective part, because our intellectual knowledge takes its beginning from the senses; and the soul itself is called the mother of all its powers, affections and actions, because they flow from it, and it is their subject and origin. The inner senses also, with their imaginings and tumults, bring forth various hindrances to the mind's recollection and devotion. For this reason the soul has need to guard herself by her higher powers and to govern her lower powers.

paras.t: Propterea subdit: Posuerunt me custodem in vineis: id est, præfati filii matris meæ compulerunt me et occasionem dederunt, ut sim custos virium mearum, interiorumque sensuum et appetituum sensitivorum: quæ vineæ appellantur, quia si debite gubernentur et excolantur, opera proferunt virtuosa, aut disponunt ad ea. Vineam meam non custodivi: id est, congeriem vinearum istarum non ita diligenter excolui, purgavi, et fecundavi, ut debui. Vinea quoque bona, est caro in spiritus servitutem redacta, dum membra ejus exhibentur arma justitiæ Deo, non arma iniquitatis peccato. Rursus principalis vinea animæ, est pars ejus intellectiva, in qua summæ Trinitatis consistit imago: quam vineam tanquam præcipuam debet anima per legem Dei ac gratiam custodire, juxta illud, Omni custodia custodi cor tuum. Verum hanc vineam non custodit, dum distractionibus immoratur, dum inordinatæ appetitioni dat locum, dum januam mentis aperit hosti, aut rei consentit illicitæ, et coram Deo negligenter se habet, ipsamque dominam ab ancilla, id est intellectivam a sensitiva, superari permittit: quod anima amorosa et sancta interdum se fecisse ac permisisse, non immerito lamentatur.
paras.en: Therefore she adds: [[1:5|they have made me the keeper in the vineyards|Posuerunt me custodem in vineis]]: that is, the aforesaid sons of my mother have compelled me and given me occasion to be the keeper of my powers, of my inner senses and of my sensitive appetites: and these are called vineyards because, if they are duly governed and tilled, they bring forth virtuous works, or dispose to them. [[1:5|my vineyard I have not kept|Vineam meam non custodivi]]: that is, I have not tilled, cleansed and made fruitful the whole of these vineyards as diligently as I ought. A good vineyard, too, is the flesh brought into subjection to the spirit[[1 Cor 9:27||]], when its members are presented as [[Rom 6:13|instruments of justice unto God|arma justitiæ Deo]], not as [[Rom 6:13|instruments of iniquity unto sin|arma iniquitatis peccato]]. Again, the chief vineyard of the soul is its intellective part, in which the image of the most high Trinity resides: and this vineyard, as the principal one, the soul must keep by the law of God and by grace, according to the words: [[Prov 4:23|With all watchfulness keep thy heart|Omni custodia custodi cor tuum]]. But she does not keep this vineyard when she lingers in distractions, when she gives room to disordered desire, when she opens the door of the mind to the enemy, or consents to something unlawful, and bears herself negligently before God, and lets the mistress be overcome by the handmaid, that is, the intellective part by the sensitive: and the loving and holy soul not without reason laments that she has sometimes done and allowed this.

paras.t: Indica mihi, quem diligit anima mea, id est ego ipsa, quæ mei sum juris per liberi usum arbitrii; vel, Anima mea, id est vita mea animalis seu spiritualis; ubi pascas, ubi cubes in meridie, id est, in quibus mentibus tam triumphantis quam militantis Ecclesiæ commoreris, eas salubriter nutriendo, atque in eis per lumen contemplationis, aut per gloriam beatificæ fruitionis conquiescendo: quatenus ad mentes vere beatas suspirem ac pertingere properem, mentes quoque viatrices vere virtuosas et contemplativas sectari non cessem. Ne vagari incipiam post greges sodalium tuorum, id est, ne decepta, sequar multitudinem animarum errantium: quæ virtuosas se simulant, quum exsistant hypocritæ: unde sub vestimentis ovium et specie bonitatis decipiunt simplices. Et tales animæ, greges sunt tuorum sodalium, id est congregationes carnalium prælatorum præsidentiumque pravorum: qui in prælatione tecum communicant, et vicarii tui dicuntur, seque tibi cohærere affirmant, quum potius diaboli sodales esse noscantur. Vel, Sodalium tuorum, id est angelorum sanctorum, qui et reprobis præsunt, et gloriæ tuæ consortes sunt. Expositio ista non multum differt a præinducta: idcirco non immoror.
paras.en: [[1:6|Shew me, O thou whom my soul loveth|Indica mihi, quem diligit anima mea]], that is, I myself, who am my own mistress through the use of free will; or, *my soul*, that is, my animal [that is, natural, belonging to the soul as the life of the body] or spiritual life; [[1:6|where thou feedest, where thou liest in the midday|ubi pascas, ubi cubes in meridie]], that is, in which minds of the Church, triumphant as well as militant, thou dwellest, feeding them wholesomely and resting in them by the light of contemplation or by the glory of beatific fruition: so that I may sigh for the truly blessed minds and hasten to reach them, and may never cease to follow the minds still on the way that are truly virtuous and contemplative. [[1:6|lest I begin to wander after the flocks of thy companions|Ne vagari incipiam post greges sodalium tuorum]], that is, lest I be deceived and follow the multitude of straying souls, who feign to be virtuous though they are hypocrites: whence, [[Matt 7:15|in the clothing of sheep|sub vestimentis ovium]] and under a show of goodness, they deceive the simple. And such souls are the flocks of thy companions, that is, the congregations of carnal prelates and wicked superiors, who share with thee in prelacy, and are called thy vicars, and declare that they cleave to thee, though rather they are known to be the devil's companions. Or, [[1:6|thy companions|Sodalium tuorum]], that is, of the holy angels, who are set over the reprobate as well, and are sharers in thy glory. This exposition does not differ much from the one given before: so I do not dwell on it.

paras.t: Si (pro non) ignoras te, o pulchra inter mulieres: id est, quia tu, o sponsa mea, contemplativa fervensque anima, scis te superadorandæ Trinitatis imaginem, sanguine meo redemptam, per sapientiam ac virtutes reformatam, meritis copiosis fulcitam: quod totum aut certitudinaliter, aut multum probabiliter nosti; idcirco egredere in actus caritatis perfectos, et abi post vestigia gregum: id est, peccatrices animas (quæ hic mulieres vocantur, quoniam concupiscentiis muliebriter enervantur, nec virile quid per virtutum exercitia sortiuntur) noli omnino aspernari ac fugere; sed vade post eas, earum miserias et peccata considerando, quatenus ferventius deprecaris pro eis, et cordialius ipsis condoleas, mihique regratieris quod a talium societate ac pravitate te præservavi aut liberavi. Tu enim, o sponsa, tantæ es perfectionis, ut ex impiorum vitiis non scandalizeris, sed compatiaris atque proficias: imo omnia cooperantur tibi in bonum; et qui scandalizatur, pusillus est. Et pasce hædos tuos juxta tabernacula pastorum, id est, motus carnales et indomitos impetus passionum reprime, et reforma secundum sanctorum Patrum doctrinam, exempla ac jussa.
paras.en: [[1:7|If|Si]] (put for *not*) [[1:7|thou know not thyself|ignoras te]], [[1:7|O fairest among women|o pulchra inter mulieres]] [Denis takes *si ignoras* as *non ignoras*, "thou art not ignorant of thyself"; his text reads *pulchra*, "fair", where the Vulgate has *pulcherrima*, "fairest"]: that is, since thou, O my bride, contemplative and fervent soul, knowest thyself to be the image of the Trinity, to be adored above all, redeemed by my blood, re-formed by wisdom and the virtues, and upheld by abundant merits (all of which thou knowest either with certainty or with great probability), therefore [[1:7|go forth|egredere]] into perfect acts of charity, [[1:7|and follow after the steps of the flocks|et abi post vestigia gregum]]: that is, do not at all despise and flee sinful souls (who are here called women, because they are unnerved by their lusts in womanish fashion and gain nothing manly through the exercise of the virtues); but go after them, considering their miseries and sins, so that thou mayest pray for them more fervently and grieve with them more heartily, and give me thanks that I have preserved or delivered thee from their company and wickedness. For thou, O bride, art of such perfection that thou art not scandalized by the vices of the wicked, but hast compassion and makest progress: indeed [[Rom 8:28|all things work together|omnia cooperantur]] for thee [[Rom 8:28|unto good|in bonum]]; and he who is scandalized is little. [[1:7|and feed thy kids beside the tents of the shepherds|Et pasce hædos tuos juxta tabernacula pastorum]], that is, restrain the carnal movements and the untamed onsets of the passions, and reform them according to the teaching, examples and commands of the holy Fathers.

paras.t: Equitatui meo, scilicet angelis sanctis ac Sanctorum phalangis, assimilavi te, amica mea, dando tibi angelicam vitam in terris, et in Sanctorum catalogo te locando, ut dicere queas: Nostra conversatio in cœlis est. Et hoc in curribus Pharaonis, id est per hoc, quod contra aciem vitiorum ac dæmonum victorialiter restitisti.
paras.en: [[1:8|To my company of horsemen|Equitatui meo]], namely to the holy angels and to the ranks of the Saints, [[1:8|have I likened thee, O my love|assimilavi te, amica mea]], giving thee an angelic life on earth and setting thee in the roll of the Saints, so that thou canst say: [[Phil 3:20|our conversation is in heaven|Nostra conversatio in cœlis est]]. And this [[1:8|in Pharao's chariots|in curribus Pharaonis]], that is, through this: that thou hast victoriously withstood the battle line of the vices and of the demons.

paras.t: Pulchræ sunt genæ tuæ sicut turturis. Habet et anima faciem suam spiritualem internam, videlicet trium superiorum virium suarum coaptationem et connexionem, seu ipsum intellectum, memoriam, voluntatem, comproportionatas: cujus faciei genæ possunt dici, intellectus speculativus et practicus, seu intellectus agens atque possibilis. Quum ergo intellectus speculativus contemplationi insistit cum casto et sapientiali pudore propriæ parvitatis, erubescens tam imperfectus ac modicus increatæ menti majestatis immensæ se repræsentare; dumque intellectus practicus virtuosis vacat operibus cum pia erubescentia, propter mala admixta et imperfectionem hujusmodi operum: tunc genæ sponsæ istius instar turturis sunt laudabiliter verecundæ, carentque amaritudinis felle et suspicionis veneno, et amant secretum, et sponso cœlesti conservant fidelitatem, qui loquitur per Prophetam: Ducam eam in solitudinem, et loquar ad cor ejus. Hinc ait Gregorius: Turtur, postquam parem suum amiserit semel, nunquam se alteri jungit, sed semper solitarie habitans, in gemitu perseverat: quoniam quem diligebat quærens, non invenit. Sic sancta anima a sponso adhuc absens, ab ejus amore non recedit, sed in ejus desiderio anhelat et gemit. Hinc hortatur Bernardus: O sancta anima, esto sola; illi soli serva te ipsam, quem tibi ex omnibus et præ omnibus elegisti; fuge publicum, fuge ipsos domesticos, secede ab amicis et inimicis. An ignoras te pudicum sponsum habere, et qui nequaquam velit ceteris suam exhibere præsentiam? Secede igitur mente, intentione et devotione, et spiritu magis quam corpore.
paras.en: [[1:9|Thy cheeks are beautiful as the turtledove's|Pulchræ sunt genæ tuæ sicut turturis]]. The soul too has her own inward spiritual face, namely the fitting together and joining of her three higher powers, or the intellect, memory and will themselves, in due proportion to one another: and the cheeks of this face may be said to be the speculative and the practical intellect, or the agent and the possible intellect [the scholastic terms for the intellect as active, making things understandable, and as receiving what it understands]. When, then, the speculative intellect applies itself to contemplation with a chaste and wise shame at its own littleness, blushing that, so imperfect and slight, it presents itself to the uncreated mind of immense majesty; and while the practical intellect gives itself to virtuous works with a holy blush, because of the evils mixed in them and the imperfection of such works: then the cheeks of this bride are, like the turtledove's, praiseworthily modest; they are free of the gall of bitterness and the venom of suspicion, they love solitude, and they keep faith with the heavenly bridegroom, who speaks by the Prophet: I [[Osee 2:14|will lead her into the wilderness: and I will speak to her heart|Ducam eam in solitudinem, et loquar ad cor ejus]]. Hence Gregory says: The turtledove, once it has lost its mate, never joins itself to another, but, always dwelling alone, perseveres in mourning, because, seeking the one it loved, it has not found him. So the holy soul, still absent from the bridegroom, does not draw back from his love, but pants and mourns in desire of him. Hence Bernard exhorts: O holy soul, be alone; keep thyself for him alone whom thou hast chosen for thyself out of all and before all; flee the public, flee even those of thine own household, withdraw from friends and enemies. Knowest thou not that thou hast a modest bridegroom, who will by no means show his presence to others? Withdraw, then, in mind, in intention and in devotion, and in spirit rather than in body.

paras.t: Collum tuum sicut monilia. Quemadmodum solus intellectus omnium exteriorum sensuum nominibus designatur (ipse enim est visus seu oculus, quo veritas cernitur; ipse est auditus interior, quo verbum Dei mente percipitur; ipse gustus, quo summæ bonitatis dulcedo sentitur et cibus animæ degustatur; ipse olfactus, quo odor virtutum hauritur; ipse tactus, quo verbum vitæ attingitur et tractatur); sic intellectus est gena et os ac collum, secundum varias suas proprietates et actiones, quibus exterioribus collo, ori, genæ assimilatur. Est itaque collum, in quantum ad superiora erigitur, ac sua erectione a fonte totius veritatis panem intelligentiæ, gratiam contemplationis, veritatis refectionem, attrahit ac sortitur. Hoc collum est sicut monilia, quando in sua illuminatione et contemplatione ornatur humilitate et sui ipsius profundissima dejectione, nec arescit elatione aut vanitate, sicut is de quo in Job legitur, Cucurrit adversus Deum erecto collo.
paras.en: [[1:9|thy neck as jewels|Collum tuum sicut monilia]]. Just as the intellect alone is designated by the names of all the outer senses (for it is the sight or eye by which truth is seen; it is the inner hearing by which the word of God is perceived in the mind; it is the taste by which the sweetness of the supreme goodness is felt and the food of the soul is tasted; it is the smell by which the fragrance of the virtues is drawn in; it is the touch by which the word of life is reached and handled), so the intellect is cheek and mouth and neck, according to its various properties and actions, by which it is likened to the outward neck, mouth and cheek. It is a neck, then, in so far as it is lifted up to higher things, and by being lifted up draws in and obtains from the fountain of all truth the bread of understanding, the grace of contemplation and the refreshment of truth. This neck is as jewels when, in its illumination and contemplation, it is adorned with humility and the deepest abasement of itself, and does not wither with pride or vanity, like him of whom we read in Job: [[Job 15:26|He hath run against him with his neck raised up|Cucurrit adversus Deum erecto collo]] [Denis reads *adversus Deum*, "against God", where the Vulgate has *adversus eum*, "against him"].

paras.t: Murænulas aureas faciemus tibi, vermiculatas argento. De muræna atque murænula, et qualiter per murænulam istam intelligatur distincta ac permixta notitia Scripturarum, dicendum est. Itaque per murænulam in hoc loco accipitur sapientialis illuminatio mentis de divinis: cui miscetur consideratio propriæ parvitatis ac rerum notitia creatarum. Talis quippe illuminatio aurea est, in quantum concernit divina; sed permiscetur quasi colori argenti, secundum quod respicit res creatas: estque menti valde necessaria illuminatio de utroque, ut agnoscat non solum excellentiam Creatoris, sed et vanitatem ac dependentiam creaturæ, et insufficientiam vilitatemque sui ipsius. Hinc S. Franciscus non solum mente raptus, sed et corpore elevatus in aere, in contemplatione altissima constitutus, clamavit: O Deus meus, quid tu, quid ego? Atque, ut postea fatebatur, aperti fuerunt ei duo libri, id est illuminatio duplex, in qua et Dei sublimitatem, et propriam defectuositatem cum ingenti admiratione conspexit.
paras.en: [[1:10|We will make thee chains of gold, inlaid with silver|Murænulas aureas faciemus tibi, vermiculatas argento]] [*murænulæ*, "little lampreys": necklaces of gold links shaped like a small eel, the *muræna*]. Of the *muræna* and the *murænula*, and of how by this *murænula* a distinct and intermingled knowledge of the Scriptures is understood, something must be said. In this place, then, by the *murænula* is meant the wise illumination of the mind about divine things, with which is mingled the consideration of one's own littleness and the knowledge of created things. Such illumination is golden in so far as it concerns divine things; but it is mixed, as it were, with the colour of silver according as it looks to created things: and illumination about both is very necessary to the mind, that it may know not only the excellence of the Creator, but also the vanity and dependence of the creature, and its own insufficiency and vileness. Hence St. Francis, not only rapt in mind but lifted up bodily into the air, set in the highest contemplation, cried out: O my God, what art thou, and what am I? And, as he afterwards confessed, two books were opened to him, that is, a twofold illumination, in which he beheld with great wonder both the sublimity of God and his own defectiveness.

paras.t: Dum esset rex in accubitu suo, nardus mea dedit odorem suum. Deus, rex noster ante sæcula, invariabilis, et bonorum nostrorum non indigens, utpote in se ipso infinite perfectus et deliciosus, quasi sitire videtur, dum nostram salutem desiderat. Unde in Deuteronomio per Moysen ait: Quis det talem eos habere mentem, ut timeant me, et bene sit eis? Qui et per alium Prophetam effatur, dicens: Utinam attendisses mandata mea. Hinc dum sanctis et salubribus actibus occupamur, a nobis reficitur, et nostro profectui congratulatur. Itaque, Dum esset rex in accubitu suo, id est, dum Dominus et Salvator in mente mea mecum cœnaret atque reficeretur, nardus mea dedit odorem suum, id est, humilitas mea erupit in actum sublimem, et suavitatem Regi gratissimam mox diffundit. Nusquam etenim anima clarius proprias deprehendit defectuositates, ærumnas et culpas, nisi dum rapitur in lucem contemplationis, qua intuetur puritatem ac majestatem prorsus incircumscriptam luminis increati: quod quanto acutius contemplatur, eo plus parvipendit ac deprimit semetipsam. Hinc patriarcha Abraham coram majestate adsistens: Loquar, inquit, ad Dominum, quum sim pulvis et cinis.
paras.en: [[1:11|While the king was at his repose, my spikenard sent forth the odour thereof|Dum esset rex in accubitu suo, nardus mea dedit odorem suum]]. God, [[Ps 73:12|our king before ages|rex noster ante sæcula]], unchangeable and having no need of our goods[[Ps 15:2||]], being in himself infinitely perfect and full of delight, seems as it were to thirst when he desires our salvation. Hence he says by Moses in Deuteronomy: [[Deut 5:29|Who shall give them to have such a mind, to fear me|Quis det talem eos habere mentem, ut timeant me]], and [[Deut 5:29|that it may be well with them|bene sit eis]]? And by another Prophet he declares: [[Is 48:18|O that thou hadst hearkened to my commandments|Utinam attendisses mandata mea]]. Hence, when we are busy with holy and wholesome acts, he is refreshed by us and rejoices at our progress. So, [[1:11|While the king was at his repose|Dum esset rex in accubitu suo]] [*accubitus*, the reclining at table], that is, while the Lord and Saviour was supping with me in my mind and being refreshed, [[1:11|my spikenard sent forth the odour thereof|nardus mea dedit odorem suum]], that is, my humility broke out into a lofty act and at once spread abroad a sweetness most pleasing to the King. For nowhere does the soul more clearly detect her own defects, miseries and faults than when she is rapt into the light of contemplation, in which she beholds the purity and wholly unbounded majesty of the uncreated light: and the more keenly she contemplates it, the more she makes little of herself and casts herself down. Hence the patriarch Abraham, standing before the majesty: [[Gen 18:27|I will speak|Loquar]], he says, [[Gen 18:27|to my Lord, whereas I am dust and ashes|ad Dominum, quum sim pulvis et cinis]].

paras.t: Fasciculus myrrhæ, dilectus meus mihi. Sponsus iste habet non solum amabilitatem dulcissimam, sed et metuendam justitiam, ac imperscrutabilem et superterribilem judiciorum profunditatem. Sponsa autem non semper unitur uniformiter suo sponso, sed interdum ut suavi, pulchro ac gratiosissimo sponso; aliquando autem contemplatur eum ut metuendum et inflexibilem judicem, de quo quisque incertus est an acceptus sit ei, finaliterve salvandus, præsertim quum comparative loquendo, salventur tam pauci. Et juxta hanc considerationem, fit ei dilectus quasi myrrhæ fasciculus, id est bonæ amaritudinis, angustiæ ac mœroris objectum et causa. Rursus, anima zelo divini honoris accensa, videns Regem ac sponsum superhonorabilissimum a multis despici, inhonorari, relinqui, gravi mœrore afficitur, amaritudinibusque impletur. Nam et miseris ita agentibus, ac se ipsos perdentibus, vehementer compatitur, sicut Apostolus qui testatur: Quis scandalizatur, et ego non uror? Sicque dilectus fit ei myrrhæ fasciculus. Verum hanc piam, amorosam et sanctam sponsæ afflictionem sponsus celeriter consolatur, et de suorum judiciorum dispositione facit eam contentam. Præcipue quoque eam oblectat, dum convertit iniquos et mundanos, quos ad virtuosam ac religiosam conversationem perducit: et tunc sponsa dicere habet: Botrus Cypri, dilectus meus mihi.
paras.en: [[1:12|A bundle of myrrh is my beloved to me|Fasciculus myrrhæ, dilectus meus mihi]]. This bridegroom has not only a most sweet loveliness, but also a justice to be feared, and an unsearchable and more than terrible depth of judgements. And the bride is not always united to her bridegroom in the same way, but sometimes as to a sweet, beautiful and most gracious bridegroom; at other times she contemplates him as a judge to be feared and unbending, of whom each one is uncertain whether he is accepted by him or is to be saved in the end, especially since, comparatively speaking, so few are saved[[Matt 20:16||]]. And according to this consideration the beloved becomes to her as a bundle of myrrh, that is, the object and cause of a good bitterness, of anguish and of grief. Again, the soul on fire with zeal for God's honour, seeing the King and bridegroom, worthy of honour above all, despised, dishonoured and forsaken by many, is struck with heavy grief and filled with bitterness. For she also has great compassion on the wretches who act so and destroy themselves, like the Apostle, who testifies: [[2 Cor 11:29|Who is scandalized, and I am not on fire|Quis scandalizatur, et ego non uror]]? And so the beloved becomes to her a bundle of myrrh. But this devout, loving and holy affliction of the bride the bridegroom quickly consoles, and he makes her content with the ordering of his judgements. Above all he delights her when he converts the wicked and worldly, and leads them to a virtuous and religious way of life: and then the bride can say: [[1:13|A cluster of cypress my love is to me|Botrus Cypri, dilectus meus mihi]].

paras.t: Insuper dum universa quæ Christus pro nobis sustinuit, anima virtuosa in unum recolligit, et congregatione unius fasciculi colligata, suæ hæc memoriæ tenacissime indelebiliterque infigit, dicere potest: Fasciculus myrrhæ, dilectus meus mihi, inter ubera mea commorabitur. Porro, dum omnem felicitatem ac gloriam sponsi sui, tam increatam secundum quod Deus est, quam creatam secundum naturam ejus assumptam, considerat; tunc ei idem dilectus est botrus Cypri: prout hic sensus ex præcedenti expositione clarius innotescit.
paras.en: Moreover, when the virtuous soul gathers together into one all that Christ suffered for us, and, binding it together as in a single bundle, fixes it in her memory most firmly and indelibly, she can say: [[1:12|A bundle of myrrh is my beloved to me|Fasciculus myrrhæ, dilectus meus mihi]], [[1:12|he shall abide between my breasts|inter ubera mea commorabitur]]. Further, when she considers all the happiness and glory of her bridegroom, both the uncreated, according as he is God, and the created, according to the nature he assumed, then the same beloved is to her [[1:13|a cluster of cypress|botrus Cypri]]: as this sense appears more clearly from the preceding exposition.

paras.t: Ecce tu pulchra es, amica mea, ecce tu pulchra. Quam ineffabiliter supernaturalia dona, videlicet gratia gratificans, et virtutes infusæ, ac septem dona Spiritus Sancti et actus eorum, ornent, pulchrificent atque nobilitent animam; quam etiam indicibiliter vitia eam vilificent ac deforment: hinc elucescit, quod anima virtuosa vocatur et est sponsa, filia et amica, heres ac soror Dei ac sponsi æterni, cui retribuitur pro mercede felicitas æternalis; anima vero vitiosa, inimica est Dei, atque adultera, filia, membrum, ancilla diaboli, cui æterna damnatio juste infligitur. Qualiter autem habeat anima pulchritudinem naturalem, in quantum ad Creatoris sui imaginem est creata, et multo præclariorem pulchritudinem per charismata gratiæ ac venustatem in moribus, ex præcedenti expositione de facili trahitur.
paras.en: [[1:14|Behold thou are fair, O my love, behold thou are fair|Ecce tu pulchra es, amica mea, ecce tu pulchra]]. How unspeakably the supernatural gifts, namely sanctifying grace [*gratia gratificans*, the grace that makes the soul pleasing to God], the infused virtues, and the seven gifts of the Holy Ghost with their acts, adorn, beautify and ennoble the soul, and how unutterably the vices debase and disfigure her, is made plain by this: that the virtuous soul is called, and is, the bride, daughter and friend, heir and sister of God, the eternal bridegroom, and eternal happiness is given her as her reward; while the vicious soul is the enemy of God, and an adulteress, the daughter, member and handmaid of the devil, and eternal damnation is justly inflicted on her. How the soul has a natural beauty, in so far as she is created to the image of her Creator, and a far more splendid beauty through the gifts of grace and comeliness of conduct, may easily be drawn from the preceding exposition.

paras.t: Ecce tu pulcher es, dilecte mi, et decorus. Tu quippe, o sponse, pulchritudinem meam commendas; sed ego in tua potius quam in mea pulchritudine glorior, tuum decorem, teque speciosissimum libentissime prorsus intueor: quia te magis quam me diligo, et in tuæ pulchritudinis intuitione, mea consistit beatitudo, atque ex pulchritudinis tuæ consideratione multiplex mihi oritur fructus, gaudium spirituale in Domino, congratulatio amorosa. Etenim tuam sanctitatem, sapientiam, perfectionem pensando, meam in omnibus imperfectionem, defectuositatemque cerno, et tui comparatione jugiter mihi vilesco. Hinc utile et salubre est, se ipsum respectu sanctiorum ac perfectiorum attendere: quatenus illorum comparatione, tanto plus se unusquisque humiliet, quanto se illis imperfectiorem ac defectuosiorem cognoscit.
paras.en: [[1:15|Behold thou art fair, my beloved, and comely|Ecce tu pulcher es, dilecte mi, et decorus]]. Thou, O bridegroom, praisest my beauty; but I glory in thy beauty rather than in mine, and most gladly gaze upon thy comeliness and upon thee, most beautiful: for I love thee more than myself, and my blessedness lies in beholding thy beauty, and from the consideration of thy beauty a manifold fruit springs up for me, spiritual joy in the Lord and loving rejoicing with thee. For in weighing thy holiness, wisdom and perfection I see my imperfection and defectiveness in all things, and in comparison with thee I grow ever more worthless in my own eyes. Hence it is useful and wholesome to regard oneself in comparison with those holier and more perfect, so that in comparison with them each may humble himself the more, the more imperfect and defective than they he knows himself to be.

paras.t: Lectulus noster floridus. Quare non ait, Lectus noster, sed tanti sponsi repausatorium, nominat lectulum? Et respondendum, quod aliqua possunt exprimi diminutive multis ex causis, videlicet ratione urbanitatis, ratione præcipuæ dilectionis, ratione magnæ humiliationis: et omnibus modis his, diminutive hic dicitur lectulus. Aliquando etiam ratione vilificationis, quandoque ad insinuandum in alio gradum suæ parvitatis aut inferioritatis. Rursus ad designandum sponsi istius immensitatem, dicitur lectulus: quia respectu tanti sponsi, parvus est omnis, quo quiescere potest, locus etiam spiritualis. Unde et in Isaia legitur: Coangustatum est stratum. Lectulus iste quis sit, dictum est in præcedenti articulo.
paras.en: [[1:15|Our bed is flourishing|Lectulus noster floridus]]. Why does she not say *lectus noster*, "our bed", but call the resting place of so great a bridegroom *lectulus*, "little bed"? The answer is that things can be expressed by a diminutive for many reasons, namely for courtesy, for special love, for great humility: and in all these ways the diminutive *lectulus* is used here.
